title: Raiders, Chiefs coaching staff matching wits will be quite the sight
summary: Klint Kubiak versus Steve Spaguolo. Andy Reid versus Rob Leonard. That set of coaching battles highlight’s the Week 4 clash between the host Las Vegas Raiders and visiting Kansas City Chiefs this Sunday inside Allegiant Stadium. Kubiak and Reid, the pair of head coaches who are also the primary offensive play callers for their respective […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Klint Kubiak versus Steve Spaguolo. Andy Reid versus Rob Leonard. That set of coaching battles highlight’s the Week 4 clash between the host Las Vegas Raiders and visiting Kansas City Chiefs this Sunday inside Allegiant Stadium. Kubiak and Reid, the pair of head coaches who are also the primary offensive play callers for their respective Raiders and Chiefs will match wits with their defensive counterparts in Leonard and Spagnuolo. What a sight that will be. Both longtime AFC West foes are atop the division with twin 3-0 records and after Sunday’s tilt, only one will reign as the top team. (Unless, of course, they end up in a tie ballgame). Not only are the overall records identical, but how many points Las Vegas and Kansas City scored and allowed in the initial three games of the 2026 season are nearly similar with the Chiefs dropping 88 points while limiting opponents to 50. Flip to the Raiders and it’s also 88 points scored while yielding 54. Kansas City is 2-0 at home and 1-0 on the road and it’s the opposite for Las Vegas as the team is 2-0 away from Allegiant Stadium and 1-0 in the home venue. Interestingly enough, hearing how the respective coaching staffs speak about one another is … identical. Be it a Raiders or Chiefs coach, the words “aggressive” and “fast” are spoken with respect — be it the offense, defense, or even special teams. Listen to Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy describe the Raiders: "It is the Raider week." Eric Bieniemy describes the challenges of facing this 3-0 Raiders team. He tells @Leabonics , "Those guys are playing fast. They're playing hard." pic.twitter.com/l2drgWkg3X — Sports Radio 810 WHB (@SportsRadio810) October 1, 2026 Here’s what Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko said when asked about what it’s like preparing for the Chiefs defense: “They’re, like I said before, an unbelievably well-coached team that plays fast. They’re very aggressive. They have great players, so it’s a tremendous challenge for us going forward.” While Kansas City struggled mightily in 2025 with a 6-11 overall record and Reid’s first losing season after 12 consecutive years of winning records — including a trio of Super Bowl victories — the reloaded and retooled Chiefs have rebounded well. And Kubiak isn’t one to harp on the 2025 campaign considering the impressive history that preceded what appears to be an anomaly of a year. “Yeah, every year, I’d say they’re the best coached unit in the league. It shows on tape,” Las Vegas rookie head coach said of the Chiefs defense. Janocko, who doesn’t call the plays but is one of Kubiak’s most trusted assistants and helps develop the offense, made no bones about Spagnuolo’s group. “He’s been doing it for a long time, and he’s been doing stuff really well for a long time,” the Raiders offensive coordinator said. “That group’s been together. They’re cohesive. They’re unbelievably well coached. Everybody knows how to do what they ask to do and do it at a fast-paced level. It’s a tremendous challenge for us.” For the Silver & Black to continue it’s turnaround this season, playing well against and defeating a team like the Chiefs helps further cement the culture change occurring in the desert. Spagnuolo has the experience and players to stymie Kubiak’s offense. The defensive boss is keen on making opponents one dimensional and Spags seeks to make the Raiders’ run game moot while also looking to either take away or limit elite tight end Brock Bowers. The Chiefs defensive mastermind is adept at using simulated pressures with heavy blitz looks and either bringing the pain or dropping back into coverage. And he’s got the talent at all three levels of the defense to do so. Steve Spagnuolo on CB L'Jarius Sneed: “He brings an element to our defense that every coordinator likes. He's a nasty, tough guy that plays hard and fast.” Adds: “Quite frankly, because I know he's out there, I'll put those guys in situations and I trust he's gonna get it… pic.twitter.com/CFCFPucQyz — KC Sports Network (@KCSportsNetwork) September 24, 2026 Kubiak, who has held a variety of positions during his coaching career before landing the head coach gig in Las Vegas, hasn’t beaten a Spagnuolo-orchestrated defense in his various capacities and stops: Chiefs 26, New Orleans Saints 13 (October 7, 2024): Kubiak was the Saints offensive coordinator. Chiefs 25, San Francisco 49ers 22 (Super Bowl, February 11, 2024): Kubiak was the 49ers pass game coordinator. Chiefs 27, Denver Broncos 24 (January 1, 2023): Kubiak was the Broncos pass game coordinator. Chiefs 34, Broncos 28 (December 11, 2022): Kubiak was the Broncos pass game coordinator. Flip the coin over to Leonard’s Raiders defense against Reid’s offense and it’s a similar neophyte versus grizzled veteran. Now, don’t get me wrong, Leonard is no stranger to Reid having been on Las Vegas staff since the 2023 season (brought on as defensive line coach) before his elevation to defensive coordinator this past offseason by Kubiak. Which makes Leonard’s comments on the Chiefs offense not surprising. “Pick your poison. 15 (quarterback Patrick Mahomes), 87 (tight end Travis Kelce), 9 (running back Kenneth Walker III), I mean, there’s a lot going,” Leonard said. “When you have good players, it’s hard to take them all away. He’s been a really good player for a long time, and his connection with Mahomes is so obvious I think to everybody, and he’s a great player.” Like his counterpart on the opposite sideline, Leonard has deployed some devious defense for the Raiders thus far using simulated pressures, showing heavy blitz, before having his defensive tackles drop back in coverage to confuse quarterbacks. That said, secure wrap-up tackling alongside playing fast, loose, aggressive, and attacking the football — something that Las Vegas is doing remarkably well with a league-leading nine takeaways — will be quite the balancing act against a well-coaching and experienced Chiefs offense conducted by Reid. “Yeah, don’t play stupid. You know what I mean?,” Leonard said describing balancing freedom and playing disciplined football. “Like there’s a difference of playing with your hair on fire and playing the game between the whistle and doing things the right way. You just focus on doing things the right way. And I think that starts with Klint. He’s done an outstanding job of that, and our guys have responded. And it’s easy for me, I just echo the message of the head coach.” Las Vegas Raiders QB Kirk Cousins Mahomes Challenge #raiders #raidernation #LasVegasRaiders #nfl #lasvegasraidersonsi pic.twitter.com/KozIE9Lfqw — Hondo Carpenter (@HondoCarpenter) October 1, 2026 Despite having success against Kubiak historically, this is no cake walk for Spagnuolo and his Chiefs defense combating the Raiders’ offense. Despite struggling at times to get traction in the run game, Kubiak isn’t shying away from giving his running backs totes and there’s a solid balance in ground and pound and aerial attack. And Las Vegas has a veteran quarterback of their own in Kirk Cousins that’s playing lights out in the first three games with a league-leading nine passing touchdowns. “Yeah, big challenge. I’ve been down this road before. Kirk’s one of these quarterbacks I’ve got a tremendous amount of respect for. He’s been doing it for a long time. I think he’s a quality guy. Every time I see him, I tell him how much I respect his character,” Spagnuolo said when asked about Cousins on Thursday. “That part is great, but the part on the football field, he gets the ball out so quick that he makes it really difficult. I think the knocking down of passes will be really important. The sticky coverage and making him throw it into tight windows will be really big. “When we do that, we need a couple of knockdowns by a corner or a safety to get him in a longer down the distance or get us off the field. We’ll have to mix it up, but I think you’ve got to be a little bit…

title: Raiders Week 4: The Chiefs Las Vegas must stop in key AFC West showdown
summary: The clash of AFC West unbeatens is set to dominate the afternoon NFL-viewing world this coming Sunday — and for good reason. The 3-0 Las Vegas Raiders play host to the 3-0 Kansas City Chiefs in an intriguing Week 4 showdown in the desert. The surging Silver & Black led by rookie head coach Klint […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Arjoon/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images). | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The clash of AFC West unbeatens is set to dominate the afternoon NFL-viewing world this coming Sunday — and for good reason. The 3-0 Las Vegas Raiders play host to the 3-0 Kansas City Chiefs in an intriguing Week 4 showdown in the desert. The surging Silver & Black led by rookie head coach Klint Kubiak welcome the capable Chiefs captained by veteran Andy Reid in a contest that’ll shape up the division just four games into the 2026 campaign. And, according to 506 Sports, the 1:25 p.m. matchup covers much of the national broadcast map for CBS . A good old-fashion slugfest is likely on the horizon when the Raiders go toe-to-toe with the incoming Chiefs. Heading into this division tilt, Las Vegas and Kansas City rank fifth and sixth in rushing attempts amongst the 32 teams with only one carry separating the two teams. It’s no secret that Kubiak — the Raiders offensive play caller — alongside his trusted offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko and offensive line coach Rick Dennison love running the football. The 93 rushing attempts is a testament to that. Flip it to Reid alongside his offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy and offensive line boss Andy Heck, and the love for the ground game is equally as feverish. The 92 rushing attempts signifies that. “Talking about Mahomes & Kelce, we just gotta make sure we’re on the things we’ve got to handle. Belief is a superpower, we wanna win every game.” Raiders LB Nakobe Dean talks about matching up with Chiefs starts Patrick Mahomes, Travis Kelce & Kenneth Walker, as well as playing… pic.twitter.com/IEMYQfWoV3 — Vegas Sports Today (@VegasSportsTD) September 30, 2026 Balanced & Brutal We established the affinity both the Raiders and Chiefs have for running the ball, but the two squads showcase a balanced offensive attack which makes both difficult to defend. While they may be in the middle of the NFL pack in passing attempts, Kansas City has thrown the ball 98 times in the trio of games heading into Week 4. Las Vegas, on the other hand, three notches below at 92 total pass attempts on the young season. Comparatively, the Chiefs completed 68.4 percent of the attempts while the Raiders are at 67.4 percent. So not only will Rob Leonard’s Las Vegas defense have to contend with the aerial attack paced by the accomplished Patrick Mahomes, they’ll have to deal with his backfield mate, running back Kenneth Walker III — a powerful and elusive ball carrier that Kubiak is all too familiar with as he dialed up plays for Walker when both were Seattle Seahawks last season. This is the inherent difference between Reid’s and Kubiak’s ground game: Kansas City has more yards (460) and a larger yards per carry average (5.0), than Las Vegas (300 yards, a paltry 3.2 yards per carry average), in comparison. Well built at 5-foot-9 and 211 pounds, the 25-year-old Walker has 360 yards on 65 totes and three touchdowns rushing while adding 82 more yards on 11 receptions with a pair of touchdowns. The Michigan State product boasts elite balance, low center of gravity, and explosiveness to evade, elude, and break through would-be tackles. Raiders defenders must be able to wrap up and tackle and when the whiffs come, bank on the team’s ability to rally and swarm to the ball. Walker presents a supreme challenge for the Raiders defense at all three levels and the meeting between the Chiefs tailback and Raiders middle linebacker Nakobe Dean is going to be a powerful one this Sunday. Rookie safety Treydan Stukes expected return to the starting lineup will help both the run defense and coverage which Mahomes is keen to exploit. Raiders center Tyler Linderbaum talks about the difficulties the Kansas City Chiefs defense presents & how the O-line is focused on improving the run game this Sunday #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/DaKtLWSodR — Raider Nation Radio (@RNR920AM) October 1, 2026 Dominate The LOS While the Chiefs may be light in the sacks department — just three so far — Las Vegas must win the battle at the line of scrimmage. If not, Steve Spagnuolo has the horses on his defense to run circles and lap Kubiak’s offense. Defensive tackle Chris Jones is still a problem — even at age 32. Standing 6-foot-6 and 310 pounds, the Mississippi State product remains a game-wrecker in the middle by collapsing the pocket and neutralizing the pass and run with his veteran savvy and physicality. He’s flanked by George Karlaftis and rookie R. Mason Thomas on the edges and both have the strengths and movement skills to mirror against Kubiak’s outside/wide zone running scheme. Behind them are are disruptive linebackers Nick Bolton and Drue Tranquill. How that duo reacts and responds to the Raiders’ pre-snap motions alongside covering the middle of the field is something to watch. And then there’s the secondary featuring cornerbacks L’Jarius Sneed and rookie Mansoor Delane. Both are sticky in coverage adn don’t be surprised if Spagnuolo tasks one or both with covering Raiders elite tight end Brock Bowers. The backend coverage from the secondary and at the second level with the linebackers gives the Chiefs the ability to be sticky and force quarterbacks to hold on to the ball which allows the defensive line to hunt. Las Vegas offensive line spearheaded by center Tyler Linderbaum and left tackle Kolton Miller will need to be on point to not only open lanes for running backs Ashton Jeanty and speedy rookie Mike Washington Jr. but also keep veteran and statue-esque quarterback Kirk Cousins with a clean pocket and upright. Las Vegas Raiders QB Kirk Cousins Mahomes Challenge #raiders #raidernation #LasVegasRaiders #nfl #lasvegasraidersonsi pic.twitter.com/KozIE9Lfqw — Hondo Carpenter (@HondoCarpenter) October 1, 2026 Head-to-Head Sunday’s clash will be the 135th meeting between the longtime AFC West foes. The Chiefs lead the all-time series 76-52-2 (74-55-2 in regular season action, 2-1 in postseason meetings) but it’s the Raiders who have the most recent victory — 14-12 this past January. Before that, Kansas City won the last three matchups with a 31-0 win last season being the most lopsided. Dating back to 2016, Las Vegas has won just four times in the 21 meetings. Quotes of Note “I think every week, you’re working on your identity, and then someone takes away your identity, takes away something you’re good at. So, you got to find multiple ways to win, and that’s what good teams do. You got to win on all three phases in order to in order to win, especially against a great team like this.” —Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak when asked about the identity of his football team “Well, I think he’s certainly fun to watch and sets a great standard for quarterback play across our league. And if they were to put up a lot of points, then you got to keep up. You also know that if if you were to get ahead, that no lead is safe. You’re just aware of how capable they are any moment of scoring points and making it hard on you as a team. So, there’s a lot of respect there, and they’ve proven it and earned that over many years. And it’ll be a great challenge for all of us on Sunday.” —Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins on the challenge Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes presents

title: Raiders Mailbag: Will Las Vegas be buyers at the NFL trade deadline?
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are gearing up for a massive Week 4 matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs, and the surprise 3-0 Raiders have a chance to finish the first quarter of the 2026 season atop the AFC West. But this week’s mailbag has a lot of questions about Las Vegas’ roster and any potential […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders are gearing up for a massive Week 4 matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs , and the surprise 3-0 Raiders have a chance to finish the first quarter of the 2026 season atop the AFC West. But this week’s mailbag has a lot of questions about Las Vegas’ roster and any potential changes, shifting the focus to that and any potential changes. Q: Do the Raiders trade for a wide receiver if they continue winning, or do they stand pat and wait for the draft to get their future No. 1? A: Someone else asked a similar question: if the Raiders are at or above .500 at the halfway point of the season, do you think they should be a buyer at the trade deadline? In my opinion, I don’t think John Spytek and Klint Kubiak should veer too far away from the offseason plan of building for the future. Sure, the Raiders are having a great season and are one of the biggest surprises in the NFL so far. But the organization’s goal was never to be good for just one year; it’s about building a sustainable winner for several years to come. So, especially if the team is at or above .500 around the trade deadline, it definitely makes sense for them to go after a young wide receiver like Brian Thomas Jr. and Marvin Harrison Jr., if they’re available. Those two are 24 years old (Thomas turns 24 next week), were highly regarded prospects, and would be under team control for two to three years since they were first-round picks and have the fifth-year option on their contracts. Obviously, Thomas and Harrison aren’t working out in their current situations; otherwise, we wouldn’t be talking about them as trade candidates. However, the Raiders would be able to get a first-round talent at a position of need at a discount, and while they’re still on relatively cheap contracts. According to Over The Cap , Thomas is making about $4 million this year and about $4.7 million in 2027 , while Harrison is making $9.6 million and $11.3 million . That’s chump change in today’s receiver market where 27 guys are making $20 million per year or more . So, if it only takes, say, a third- or fourth-round pick to get one of those guys, I think Spytek should do that, especially since the Raiders are playing their way out of Jeremiah Smith territory. Now, when it comes to adding an older veteran — Terry McLaurin and Vita Vea are a couple of names that come to mind — Spytek should be more price-sensitive, in my opinion. Would McLaurin and Vea make the Raiders a better team right now? Absolutely. However, again, don’t mortgage the future or lose sight of the long-term goal just to improve the roster for half a season and maybe one more year after that. If it’s something like a fifth-rounder or later, I can get on board with that, and you could probably sway me into a fourth. The Raiders did a great job of adding young talent this offseason, and it’s paying dividends with guys like Nakobe Dean (25, turns 26 in December), Treydan Stukes (25), Hezekiah Masses (22), etc., already playing well. If you’re asking me, veering away from that strategy and giving up significant draft capital for players who are in their 30s is a bad and short-sighted decision. But again, if Spytek can get someone like that for cheap, go for it! Q: Be honest now. Before the season, did you have the 3-0 Raiders on your bingo card? If no, what record? A: Hell no! LOL! Heading into the season, I thought they’d be 1-2 with losses to the Chargers and Saints. But trust me, no one is happier that I was wrong than I am. I underestimated how quickly Kubiak could turn the culture around, and I couldn’t be more excited for the future, including how the rest of this season plays out. Q: Will Treydan Stukes, as a more valuable starting FS, be removed from special teams duty in favor of using Isaiah Pola-Mao? The rookie’s injury risk seems too high. A: I certainly hope so because Vegas doesn’t have another good option at free safety, as we found out (and kind of already knew) once Stukes suffered the concussion against the Chargers. What does give me some worry is that Pola-Mao was already on every special teams unit in Week 1, when Stukes was also contributing on special teams. However, what gives me hope is that IPM only took three special teams snaps (all on the punt coverage team) with Stukes out last week, per Pro Football Focus . Tristin McCollum — who was active and played on special teams in Week 1 but inactive for Week 2 — filled in for IPM on special teams in New Orleans. So, it seems like the coaching staff learned its lesson and is going to keep key starters off special teams moving forward. Q: Excited to see that Stukes looks ready to play against the Chiefs. That said, why oh why did IPM play 100% of the FS snaps last week? Five catches on five targets with 3 TDs and a missed tackle, according to PFF. Any casual Raiders fan could’ve told Rob Leonard to expect those results. He couldn’t rotate Tristin McCollum in for a couple of drives here or there? Really? Where is Dalton Johnson? Would you rather see IPM at free safety than Dalton? IPM is a fantastic backup box safety, but I’m done seeing him at the back of our defense. A: I hear ya, but the only person who can give you a truthful or non-speculative answer to a lot of your questions here is Rob Leonard. My take on the matter is that McCollum absolutely should have gotten a chance to play last week. I don’t know if the results would have been much different because he isn’t a good free safety either, but Pola-Mao obviously wasn’t getting the job done. Leonard might as well give someone else a shot at that point, whether that be McCollum or another defensive back on the roster. As for Johnson, he’s been a healthy scratch every game so far. Apparently, the coaching staff doesn’t think he’s ready to see the field, especially since last week would have been a great opportunity for him to dress for the first time. I will say that Johnson profiles more as a big nickel or box safety; however, as you pointed out, so does Pola-Mao. Luckily, Stukes is back for Sunday, so this shouldn’t be an issue moving forward. Hopefully, if he does have to miss time down the road, Leonard learned his lesson and will give someone other than Pola-Mao a chance to patrol the back end of the defense. Q: I think Eric Stokes seems like a good teammate and loves being a Raider. He doesn’t seem like a guy who gets his contract and then stops working hard. Why do you think his game has fallen off? A: One of my concerns with Stokes is that he isn’t a good fit in the coverage scheme that Leonard is running. Stokes has a lot of linear speed, but he doesn’t have good lateral movement skills and is tight hipped, making it difficult to change directions. That’s not as big of a deal when a cornerback is playing a lot of spot dropping coverages like traditional Cover 3 and 4. However, Leonard is using a lot of pattern matching coverages. The scheme falls into the Cover 3 or Cover 4 family, but it’s different than just getting to a landmark and playing that area. I like to call pattern matching “man coveage with more rules”, where a corner will cover a receiver only if the receiver runs a certain route or reaches a certain depth. And if the receiver doesn’t cross the threshold, then the corner moves onto find another pass-catcher who fits into their coverage rules or looks to help a teammate in coverage. So, it’s kind of a hybrid between man and zone coverage, where defenders get to an area at first and then play man if a threat enters into it. That way the defense isn’t giving up as many throwing windows to the quarterback (a weakness of zone coverage) while not getting into bad matchups where a linebacker has to cover a deep route (a weakness of man coverage). Also, there are a good amount of situtaions where a corner will play pure man coverage while the rest of the defense is in zone. It’s called ‘ MEG ’, which stands for Man Everywhere he Goes, if…

(Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images I love the deep shots with Malik! Keep them up. What do you say? Obviously, deep shots keep the defenses honest. No sitting on possession routes during the whole game. If you watched the Super Bowl where the SeaPigeons destroyed the Broncos, there was a play where Peyton Manning threw a pass into the flat parallel to the line of scrimmage to a WR and Richard Sherman is covering him right there! He was NOT worried about being beat deep. Don’t forget when the opposing defense has to scheme for the deep shots, that takes their focus away from the run game and short passes. Deep shots during a real game, hopefully, will lead to increased trust and timing between Malik and the WRs. Yes, an 18-yard square-in also leads to trust and timing but I think deep shots can be just as effective. And maybe, just maybe, the deep shot will be permanent part of the offense. During the Raiders game, Malik threw an INT on a deep shot but if you look closely, he threw off his back foot. A Big IF; IF Malik steps into that throw even with the bad route (pointed out by Mark Schlereth) it is a TD. IMHO! Deep shots are fun to watch and can be de-moralizing to the defense when they hit. If you ever listened to Coach Howard Schnellenberger (who himself coached for Bear Bryant), he knew the average completion percentage for EVERY type of pass. His knowledge was scary and he had a really DEEP voice which it made his statements sound like Moses. I think he mentioned 9% for a deep shot success rate. I don’t want to get into statistics and expected probabilities etc but the Raiders won 3 Super Bowls titles throwing deep shots (Cliff Branch STILL gives me nightmares). I am not saying this is the best path forward, but I like the GUTS and BRAVADO for trying. This is for SDPhinsFan! (I think that is the handle) Keep on bringing facts: Yes, the Phins led the league in LEAST number penalties for years but that can be totaling misleading. I break penalties down into two types : pre-snap procedural stuff and the actual real penalties (pass interference, holding, late hits, etc). I do not know if the Phins had the LEAST in both of those categories. So that would be good to know. Did Shula really intimidate the refs? Perhaps! This is for everyone else! Better than the NFL! You all do realize the fans are an annoyance for the league and the owners? If they cared at all, the powers that be would fix the officiating. Maybe they think fans getting angry is good for the game, like negative publicity was for the Who and the Rolling Stones? Look at the WNBA: if you wrote this in a movie, they would say you are making this up. An evil league commissioner plots against its star player. If I am a DA, I would investigate the WNBA for collusion against Caitlin Clark and the reasons that it is allowed. I would have done the same thing for the NBA for Michael Jordan. David Stern should be in prison for what he allowed to happen to Michael Jordan. I will repeat myself: the anti-trust exemption needs to be removed from every pro sports league. After that, we subpoena the league records for the officiating (we could do this before removing the anti-trust exemption BUT this will get their attention) flaws and what the league actually thinks and why they don’t try to fix it. I know this sounds like conspiracy theory talk but I have seen Outkick articles (one by the great Armando Salguero) this week about it, so there is traction. But don’t forget that this is the good ole boy network and one phone call from Roger Goodell to the Murdoch folks and this goes away until the next officiating SNAFU, which will be tomorrow. Go Phins!

title: NFL draft prospects 2027: Players to watch in Ohio State vs. Iowa
summary: The 2026 college football schedule moves into Week 5 today, giving us another chance to look at some players who could be on the Miami Dolphins’ radar for the 2027 NFL Draft. The Dolphins will likely have a very early selection in the spring, and they may be able to take just about anyone on […]
full_text: COLUMBUS, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 19: Jeremiah Smith #4 of the Ohio State Buckeyes runs with the ball during the first quarter of a game against the Kent State Golden Flashes at Ohio Stadium on September 19, 2026 in Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Ben Jackson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 college football schedule moves into Week 5 today, giving us another chance to look at some players who could be on the Miami Dolphins’ radar for the 2027 NFL Draft. The Dolphins will likely have a very early selection in the spring, and they may be able to take just about anyone on the board. Over the past few weeks, he has highlighted games featuring players the team might target later in the draft; today, we turn to a player who could land in the first overall slot. The Big Ten has our attention today, with the fifth-ranked Ohio State Buckeyes facing the 14th-ranked Iowa Hawkeyes. It is not just a big-time conference game between two ranked teams, but it gives us a chance to take a look at wide receiver Jeremiah Smith – a Miami native who could be brought home to South Florida in 2027. Kickoff for the game is at 3:30 p.m. Eastern on CBS and Paramount+. As we have for each week of the college football schedule this year, we take a quick look at some players to watch for each team in today’s game. Ohio State 2027 Draft prospects Jeremiah Smith, wide receiver (Junior) – Smith looks like he could be the first wide receiver selected with the first-overall pick since Keyshawn Johnson in 1996, and just the fourth in league history. He brings size (6-foot-4, 225 pounds ) and explosion to the position, getting off the line fast, attacking his route, and going up to get contested balls. If the Dolphins are convinced Malik Willis is their guy at quarterback, or at least are looking to give him the 2027 season to prove himself, Smith could be their top pick, giving them a 2027 wide receiver group that would feature rookie Smith, second-year receivers Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell, and Kevin Coleman, and fourth-year receiver Malik Washington. That could be a dominating group. Bringing Smith home to Miami might be in the Dolphins’ plans. Julian Sayin, quarterback (Redshirt Sophomore) – Sayin is a pocket passer with anticipation and vision. He is a rhythm passer who uses his timing and his understanding of what the offense is trying to do to put the ball in the right place at the right time. Of course, having Smith as your top wide receiver is helpful. Could the Dolphins consider adding Smith in the first round, then selecting Sayin in the second round, giving him time to develop at the NFL level and keeping him with his top receiving target? Jaylen McClain, safety (Junior) – Moved into the starting lineup in 2025, McCalin has proven himself to be a leader on the defense, getting the secondary organized and communicating. He is a sure tackler with the range to be a very good free safety. He played in the shadow of Caleb Douglas last year, so he is working to make a name for himself this year, and he is doing well. The turnovers have not been there for him yet (he has one career interception, coming in Week 2 against Texas this year), but if he can develop that part of his game, he could be a strong centerfield option at the NFL level. He is probably a third-round option right now and could be a developmental starter with special teams value as well. Kenyatta Jackson Jr., edge (Redshirt Senior) – A long-limbed edge rusher who uses speed and power to his advantage, Jackson has good flexibility and can get into the backfield in passing situations. He has to improve his finishing, however. As he continues to work on his technique, he should only get better, especially if he adds additional options to his game, allowing him to get off of blocks if his speed does not immediately win off the snap. He is probably a day-two prospect who could continue to climb the boards based on the potential that is there. Luke Montgomery, guard (Senior) – Montgomery might be the definition of a solid guard that you forget is there – exactly what you would want in a guard. In 2025, he allowed just three sacks and was penalized twice. That is impressive over 14 games played. He is a really good prospect with room to keep growing. He could move outside to tackle if needed, but his strength is as a guard, and that is where he should land in the NFL. He has the athleticism to be a pulling guard who can get into the second level and clear a path through linebackers. A strong day-three prospect who could play his way into hearing his name called at the end of day two. Iowa 2027 Draft prospects Reece Vander Zee, wide receiver (Junior) – A big-bodied receiver (6-foot-4, 215 pounds), Vander Zee has a great catch radius and can win contested catches. He is not afraid to support the run as an outside blocker. He needs to improve his route running and be more consistent to make an immediate impact at the NFL level. He could use another year in college, but if he declares for the Draft, he is likely a late-round option who will need time to develop in the NFL while potentially adding day one special teams work. Addison Ostrenga, tight end (5th-year Senior) – Ostrenga is an in-line, blocking tight end who could work as a sixth offensive lineman and provide some possession-style receptions. He sustained an Achilles tear in early 2025, missing the majority of the season but he is back on the field this year, playing in all four games with seven receptions for 70 yards and a touchdown early in the year. There are comparisons to former Dolphins tight end Durham Smythe, and that might be a great comparison. He is probably destined to be a depth tight end at the NFL level, but there is a role for him. Zach Lutmer, cornerback (Redshirt Junior) – Lutmer is a nickel cornerback who is not afraid to get into run defense. He covers well, steps up on the edge, and blitzes when asked. He can slide outside if needed, but his strength is in the slot; he is a versatile option who tackles well and does whatever is asked of him. He needs to improve as a press-corner, and his footwork is not always clean. He has decent speed, but if he faces a true deep threat, he will probably need help over the top. He projects as a mid-round prospect who could sneak into the earlier rounds with a strong 2026 season and his upside as a special teams player Trevor Lauck, offensive tackle (Redshirt Junior) – A strong pass-protecting left tackle, Lauck looks exactly like an Iowa left tackle prospect should. He knows how to pass block; he keeps his quarterback clean and tracks his assignment through stunts and blitzes. He needs to improve as a run blocker, and his footwork can improve, especially against speed rushers. He will need time to develop at the NFL level, particularly as the speed of the game increases dramatically, but he could be a solid swing-tackle option early in his career, or he could kick inside to play guard, where he may excel in the NFL. He is probably a day three draft prospect. Hank Brown, quarterback (Redshirt Junior) – Brown looks like your old-school pocket passer. He is probably system-dependent at the NFL level who will need development time, but he could be a solid backup option who can come in and steady an offense when needed. He has had limited playing time, only becoming the starter this year, and he has to clean up his turnovers, but there are flashes of potential. He will not be a franchise quarterback, but he can be asked to take over and provide solid play when needed once he is comfortable in his professional system.

title: SB Nation Reacts Results: Vikings’ Biggest Offensive Problem Is Behind Center
summary: We’ve got the results of our SB Nation Reacts poll for this week, and since we said we’d get them to you before kickoff on Sunday. . .well, it looks like we’d better get them to you now. So, let’s get to it without any further ado. We’ll start the way we always start, with […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 27: Kyler Murray #1 and Carson Wentz #11 of the Minnesota Vikings take the field against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the game at Raymond James Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’ve got the results of our SB Nation Reacts poll for this week, and since we said we’d get them to you before kickoff on Sunday. . .well, it looks like we’d better get them to you now. So, let’s get to it without any further ado. We’ll start the way we always start, with our question about whether or not our readers feel that our Minnesota Vikings are moving in the right direction. After a season-high following an ugly win in Week 2, a second consecutive ugly win had our fans feeling quite the opposite way after the Week 3 win over Tampa Bay. After seeing the confidence number leap to 75% going into Week 3, it’s now plummeted to just 41% of fans believing the purple are heading in the right direction going into Week 4. Following yet another abysmal showing from the offense, it isn’t terribly difficult to understand why. Yes, it’s fun to watch Brian Flores’ defense continue to put the other team’s offense in a blender every week, but Minnesota’s offense seems to be in a constant state of disarray. Even when they put up 39 points in Week 1, they did so with the benefit of a lot of short fields and miscues from Green Bay rather than a big offensive performance, so things haven’t exactly been encouraging on that side of the ball. That leads us into our second question for the week, which was what our readers felt was the biggest problem with the Vikings’ offense so far through the first three weeks of the season. While there were quite a few reasons, the biggest one seems to be the most obvious one. Of those who responded to our poll, 43% felt that the biggest problem offensively thus far has been the play at quarterback, which has been split between Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz through the first three games of the season. Another 27% cited Kevin O’Connell’s system, while another 19% felt the primary issue is the playcalling. There are 7% of our respondents who feel that the reason is something that was not listed among the choices in our poll, while 4% believe the running game is the main culprit. I believe I saw some folks in the comment section of the post for this week mention the offensive line, but I’m not sure that’s the issue, to be honest. It seems like the quarterbacks have had time when they’ve needed it, but they either haven’t found people open or haven’t pulled the trigger when they’ve needed to. While the quarterback play has been mostly atrocious, this offensive system has never really had anything that resembles any kind of short, quick passing game, and it seems like the lack of it continues to hurt this offense as much as anything else. The Vikings have enough guys who can make plays in space with the ball in their hands, but they’re not giving them the opportunity to do so. That’s not on them, or even on the quarterbacks, really. It’s a product of this system as much as anything else, in my opinion. Those are our SB Nation Reacts results for this week, folks. As always, we thank everyone who took the time to participate in our poll for this week, and we’ll have another one for you early next week as well, so keep your eyes open for it. summary: Ahead of Sunday’s game at U.S. Bank Stadium against the Miami Dolphins, the Minnesota Vikings have just one practice squad elevation for this week, but with the way things have gone in the first three weeks, it could be a very important one. The Vikings have elevated punter Johnny Hekker from the practice squad, meaning […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 22: Johnny Hekker #5 of the Minnesota Vikings stands on the sidelines during an NFL preseason football game against the Baltimore Ravens at U.S. Bank Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ahead of Sunday’s game at U.S. Bank Stadium against the Miami Dolphins, the Minnesota Vikings have just one practice squad elevation for this week, but with the way things have gone in the first three weeks, it could be a very important one. The Vikings have elevated punter Johnny Hekker from the practice squad, meaning that he will handle punting and holding duties for the second week in a row as Brett Thorson continues to deal with a hamstring injury. It’s important to note that this is Hekker’s first elevation from the practice squad this year. Ahead of last week’s game against Tampa Bay, Hekker was signed from the practice squad to the 53-man roster, not elevated, so he still has two more elevations remaining after this one and will not have to be released after the game as he was last week. In last week’s game, Hekker was called upon eight times and performed well, averaging 46.5 yards with a long of 63 and placing two punts inside the 20-yard line. He also, as far as I could tell, did a solid job of holding on all three of Will Reichard’s field goal attempts and both extra points. If he hadn’t. . .well, we’d obviously know. There hasn’t been a whole lot of word on just how bad Thorson’s injury is. The team hasn’t gone as far as putting him on IR, but he hasn’t practiced for two weeks, either. I’m not sure if the team is waiting until after the bye week to get him back out there again or what’s happening, but at least they have a solid veteran option like Hekker around for instances like this one. That should be the last roster move the Vikings make before Sunday’s game. If they do make any other moves, we’ll bring them to you as soon as we’re able.

After a week where the Vikings ship J.J. McCarthy to the Giants for a 5th-rounder — Two Old Bloggers breaks down the epic QB fail. Drew Bunting sits in for Darren Campbell alongside Dave Stefano to dissect the McCarthy trade fallout, Brian Flores’ league-leading defense, Josh Oliver’s season-ending bicep tear, and a Week 4 preview against the winless Miami Dolphins. The show, a Vikings 1st & SKOL production, doesn’t hold back — and with Minnesota sitting 3-0 despite averaging just 238 yards of offense per game, there’s plenty to unpack. Dave opened with a blunt assessment of the McCarthy trade: “That’s not a retool, that’s an admission.” Drew questioned the entire quarterback development pipeline, saying [Kevin] O’Connell’s staff “couldn’t develop J.J. McCarthy,” and borrowed a poker metaphor from his Uncle Paulie: “If you haven’t figured out in 30 minutes who the weak player is, it’s you.” He pointed to the Vikings’ 5-for-28 third-down conversion rate over two weeks as evidence that KOC is “the weak player at the poker table right now.” The defense, though, is historically dominant. Chat member Justin Barkley perfectly described Brian Flores’ approach: “He will bludgeon an offense to the point of failure.” With 14 sacks and an 11.1% red zone defense, Flores’ unit is carrying the team — but Darren worries he’s too good to keep. Fan with us at Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL on the Bleav Network @BleavNetwork . title: Sunday Patriots Notes: Josh McDaniels wants offense to ‘stick with the process’
summary: The New England Patriots are taking on the Buffalo Bills on Sunday for their first division game of the 2026 season. Similar to last year, this contest could have major ramifications on Mike Vrabel’s team: at 1-2 going up against a 3-0 opponent, a victory might have a similar effect as it had on the […]
full_text: The New England Patriots are taking on the Buffalo Bills on Sunday for their first division game of the 2026 season. Similar to last year, this contest could have major ramifications on Mike Vrabel’s team: at 1-2 going up against a 3-0 opponent, a victory might have a similar effect as it had on the Patriots’ 2025 Super Bowl team. Our attention was mostly on this particular game this week, and even our weekly clean-up has a distinct Patriots vs. Bills flavor. And with that said, welcome to the Week 4 version of our Sunday Patriots Notes . Sticking with the process Through three games, the Patriots’ offense has been one of the worst in the NFL by whatever metric you want to use. Points? Tied for dead-last. Turnovers? The same. Yards? 21st. Expected points added per play? 28th. Needless to say, things have not been great. And with every unsatisfactory performance, the pressure continues to mount. Quarterback Drake Maye, who has turned the ball over a league-worst seven times so far, has been the face of New England’s offensive struggles. However, as offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels pointed out, the problems are far-reaching and it is on the entire offensive structure — players and coaches alike — to turn the ship around toward calmer waters. “Our improvement and our progress offensively is going to be a function of everybody. Starts with me, our coaches, our players,” McDaniels said. “It takes a lot of us to do the right things and call the game the way I want to call it and execute it the way they want to execute it, and do those things right, take care of the football, and then go out there and see what that looks like. We know we haven’t done that yet, and so what is the result going to be when we do it? I hope we find out on Sunday.” But while the Patriots offense has remained stuck in the mud thus far, the veteran OC is not willing to make any drastic changes. Instead, the message has been sticking to the plan in place. “Sometimes, when you get into a stretch where you want to do things so well right now and you’re just not doing them exactly the way you want them, you can feel like you want to press and drastically alter what you’re doing; when I think the solution really is not patience in the sense of being lazy to change something — that’s not what I’m referring to — but I think just sticking with the process of trying to make things right that you know you can make better,” McDaniels said. “I think our players see things that we can do better, and until we actually do the things that we’re trying to do the way we want them done, that’s where you get into trouble, where you start changing things and throwing everything out.” One of the most accomplished offensive coaches in NFL history, McDaniels oversaw an attack that was among the best in football last year before running into some trouble in the playoffs. The hope was that some savvy offseason moves and natural development within the system implemented in 2025 would help the unit get over the hump, but so far the opposite has been the case. Nonetheless, McDaniels still has confidence in the plan and his players, including Drake Maye. And even with time already seemingly starting to run out, he believes that the approach —continuously building and adding to the offense along the way — ultimately will prove to be fruitful. “Are we going to run plays that we haven’t run before this week? Yes. Did we do that last week? Yes. Is it going to be 50% of the game plan? I hope not, because I think you get good at certain things through repetition and habit,” he explained. “I think that I’m drawn on past experiences from different seasons, and sometimes it’s sticking with it and as painful as it can feel sometimes, the joy of doing it well isn’t far away.” Slow running Even though Drake Maye’s issues have been front and center, the support he has received from New England’s run game has also been underwhelming. Three games into the season, the group ranks just 24th in EPA per run (-0.205). “I think there have been flashes of some good stuff, and then some stuff we hadn’t done well,” said left tacke Will Campbell. “You just have to keep working at it to give the guys in the backfield opportunities to make plays. … Anytime you can run the football at your own will it makes the game easier regardless of any other stuff going on.” The Patriots, like last year, have relied heavily on a combination of Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson as the 1-2 punch at running back so far. Stevenson acknowledged that the production is not yet where it needs to be, and that — just like Josh McDaniels preached in regards to the offense as a whole — it takes time to get there. “It still needs work,” he said. “Obviously, it’s early in the season. But that comes down to just more reps and just running those plays; it’s me and Tre getting behind our O-line and trusting them and them trusting us.” New-look environment The Patriots have some fond memories of the Bills’ old stadium, going 32-21 through the years. On Sunday, however, they will find themselves in a different environment: the franchise’s new, state-of-the-art Highmark Stadium. For the Patriots, however, the new arena won’t have much of an impact on the atmosphere they are going to face. “I’m sure they’ll be as friendly as they were last year,” Will Campbell said. “It’ll be fun, though. Those games are always exciting. Lots of energy, a lot of juice, it’s a good atmosphere to play in.” “It’s always an incredible atmosphere,” added safety Kevin Byard. “It’s like a college town. Those fans love Buffalo, and those environments, me as a player, I always love to go to stadiums like that.” Since the NFL-AFL merger in 1970, the Patriots are 30-34 when playing a regular season game at a new opposing stadium for the first time. They did win seven straight between 2014 and 2021, but lost their two most recent such games to the Vikings and Raiders in 2022. Kicking woes Andy Borregales has not had his best season so far. The Patriots’ second-year kicker has missed field goal attempts in back-to-back games, all from a rather makable distance. What’s the issue? For special teams coordinator Jeremy Springer it all comes back to one thing. “It’s just honing down some of the fundamental things,” he explained. Borregales has had some good moments already this year, but he sent a 47-yard attempt wide to the right in Week 2 against Pittsburgh, followed by a 38-yard miss in the same direction versus Jacksonville last Sunday. “In a four-quarter game, you know you can have a great pregame and then you might not be able to kick a field goal in the third quarter,” Springer added. “It’s just honing him back and making sure that he’s locked in from the first to the fourth quarter on some of those things. He’s got to understand — as we all understand — how important those plays really are in a game. “You make that field goal, it’s a one-score game in the third quarter with some momentum. And then when you don’t make those field goals, it gets flat because we’re dependent on those guys to make those field goals and get those points, and our field goal team to block. It’s all about making him understand that you have to be locked in for four quarters. He’s working his tail off and doing great things. Unfortunately, he missed that one, but always confident in Andy. He’ll be right back to where he was as he did in the fourth quarter there, hit that field goal later to get right back on track.” Backup development With Christian Gonzalez out, the Patriots will rely on Carlton Davis and Marcus Jones as their top two cornerbacks. Charles Woods, the team’s fourth option at the position, is also likely to see increased snaps as Mike Vrabel said. For Davis, he earned that increase due to the work he put in in his second season in the system. “Just more mature, understanding how to be a better professional,” Davis said about the 26-year-old. “He’s coming into the facility earlier, he’s put…

The Miami of Ohio product remained a Titan until the 2026 league year opened. Not tendered as a restricted free agent, he signed with the Patriots in March and was retained on the practice squad at its formation after being released in August. Three standard elevations are permitted under league rules before 53-man contracts would be required to take the field. Two remain for Vildor. One remains for Brown. title: Patriots worried about ‘second play’ with Bills QB Josh Allen
summary: Josh Allen’s status as one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL is undisputed. What makes him such a dangerous and productive player is not just his arm talent, size and versatility, but how he uses a combination of his rare skills to become arguably the most frustration-inducing player in all of pro football. As […]
full_text: Josh Allen’s status as one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL is undisputed. What makes him such a dangerous and productive player is not just his arm talent, size and versatility, but how he uses a combination of his rare skills to become arguably the most frustration-inducing player in all of pro football. As long as he has the ball, after all, the Buffalo Bills have a chance. And the 30-year-old is making sure to keep that chance alive for as long as he can on every single play. This, in turn, puts immense pressure on opponents to keep defending even when a play otherwise would be long over. It is precisely what the New England Patriots have been harping on all week. “He’s going to extend plays. We know that’s going to happen. You can’t necessarily stop it, you only can contain it,” said safety Kevin Byard. “As DBs, we have to be able to cover for as long as it takes. Ten seconds — it doesn’t matter. Especially on the backend, it’s not necessarily the play that’s called, it’s the second or third play within the play. So, we’re going to have to be very mentally, but more than likely physically exhausted in this game because this team and Josh, they have no quit.” Defending the “second play” has been the Patriots’ defensive theme of the week. On the flip side, making said play has been Allen’s bread and butter since entering the NFL as a first-round draft choice out of Wyoming in 2018. The touchdown got wiped away by a hold on a downfield block, but Josh Allen doing this to you on fourth down must be the worst feeling ever. pic.twitter.com/yImsqnsymF — Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) September 28, 2026 “It’s kind of like recess football in terms of, ‘If you have a man, you have to cover your man. And if you’re free, then you have to figure out a way to get this guy with the ball either down or out of bounds,’” said Patriots cornerbacks coach Justin Hamilton. “He’s elite, and he’s as good as I can remember seeing in my lifetime. I’ve watched a lot of NFL football. I don’t know of a guy that’s better at play extension.” Allen is able to make the so-called second plays because of his size, strength and vision. He can simply evade pressure or fight through tackle attempts, all while keeping his eyes downfield for either a rushing lane or receiver to open up downfield. This is why he is typically ranked high in time-to-throw metrics and also one of the most effective scrambling quarterbacks in the league. None of that is nothing new, of course. Defending it still remains a challenge, though — one the Patriots are going up against twice a year, including this coming Sunday. “It’s the hardest thing, in my opinion, in football to have to defend,” said defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr, who referred to Allen as an “MVP-caliber quarterback playing MVP football.” For him, the secret to countering the extended play lies in the preparation. The goal is not just to know what is going to happen, but be capable of reacting in an instant without much hesitation. Kuhr used two words to describe the approach: muscle memory. “We try to rep it in practice. Tommy [DeVito] and Behren [Morton] are giving good looks,” he said. “We talk about our rules within it and we harp on it every single day, we show the film of it. Everybody’s got to know it. Everybody’s got to be on the same page. Everybody’s got to understand it, so it becomes muscle memory because he’s a special cat and he’s a different cat. You know you get to see that twice a year and it just looks different, so we have to do everything we can to make how we execute the second play muscle memory. “There can’t be any lapses of, ‘I thought the play was over.’ No, the play is never over. We have to do it for 60 minutes too — that’s the hardest part: this guy does not go away. No matter what the score is, he does not go away. So, we have to have the competitive stamina for 60 minutes, understand what our rules are to defend the second play, and we all have to be on the same page doing it, make it muscle memory.” Muscle memory is one part, game-day execution another. And for the Patriots, the latter will be difficult this week given their personnel situation. Two of their best defenders, cornerback Christian Gonzalez and defensive tackle Christian Barmore, will miss the contest on Sunday due to shoulder injuries. Under normal circumstances both would play valuable roles in keeping Allen contained through tight coverage and resetting the line of scrimmage, respectively. Without those blue-chip players, the task will be even more daunting than it already is. “It’s going to be a 60-minute ball game,” said Byard. “We could be up 35 points and he’s going to find a way to try to come back and score 40 points. This is going to be a tough challenge for us and we’re going to have to play a 60-minute complete ball game.”

title: Saints vs. Falcons: QB to QB Matchup
summary: The New Orleans Saints will see their bitter rivals enter the Superdom for a primetime matchup on Monday night as they face off against the Atlanta Falcons. The Falcons have been down on their luck, but they are certainly not lacking talent. Their offense still features some of the best young players in the league, […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: New Orleans Saints quarterback Tyler Shough (6) is sacked by Detroit Lions linebacker Derrick Barnes (55) during the Detroit Lions versus New Orleans Saints game on Sunday September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints will see their bitter rivals enter the Superdom for a primetime matchup on Monday night as they face off against the Atlanta Falcons. The Falcons have been down on their luck, but they are certainly not lacking talent. Their offense still features some of the best young players in the league, including Bijan Robinson, Drake London, and Kyle Pitts. However, they just can’t seem to find consistency at the quarterback position. Throughout the offseason, there was a quarterback battle between Michael Penix Jr. and Tua Tagovailoa. Tua actually won the job while Penix continued to recover from an injury. However, before the first game of the season, Tua suffered an injury of his own. The Falcons then turned to Cooper Rush, who started in Week 1 and 2. With the offense struggling to perform, they turned to their fourth quarterback, Jack Strand, who came in and immediately threw a pick-six against the Panthers. Finally, last week, the Falcons were able to get Penix back, and the offense showed some life. Penix’s first drive of the season also ended with an interception, but after that, the Falcons were able to surprise a lot of people by defeating the Packers on the road, 35-14. Penix was Atlanta’s starting quarterback last year but struggled to find a rhythm. This could be the year he takes a step forward. In his lone start of the season, Penix completed 18 of 25 passes (72%) for 256 yards, averaging 10.2 yards per attempt, with one touchdown and one interception. The good news for the Falcons is that they did not allow a single sack against the Packers last week, and that is something the Saints will need to change. The focus for the Saints’ defense shouldn’t necessarily be to stop Penix. If anything, it should be to force Penix to be the one who has to beat them. Bijan Robinson went off against the Packers, rushing for 194 yards and two touchdowns, while Drake London complemented the running game with nine receptions for 194 yards. He also had a long reception of 68 yards. Most of Penix’s passing production came from one receiver, while Robinson accounted for much of the offense’s remaining production. The Saints will need to generate pressure up the middle. With Penix being a left-handed quarterback, the normal pass-rushing dynamics are flipped a little. His blind side is to his right, so the Saints need to prevent him from stepping up into his throws, especially considering that he isn’t much of a threat to run. Flush him out of the pocket and force him to change his throwing spots. They will also need to take away his first read, which is usually Drake London. Force the Falcons into third-and-long situations by getting to Robinson on early downs and keeping the offense off schedule. Last year, the Saints had success against Atlanta and Bijan Robinson’s rushing attack. In two games against the Saints, Brandon Staley’s defense held Robinson to a combined 103 rushing yards and zero touchdowns. So, it’s possible. Tyler Shough and the Saints’ Offense : Tyler Shough leads the Saints nto this matchup, and had the fourth quarter against the Raiders not been played, Shough would have been coming off the best game of his young career. But football is a four-quarter sport. Through the first three games, Shough has 912 passing yards and is completing 68.9% of his passes. He also has eight touchdowns and three interceptions. The most notable thing about Shough’s stat line is that the games in which he has committed a turnover are the games the Saints have lost. Start by protecting the football. The Saints also have to help him in that regard because the pass protection has been very poor. Through the first three games, Shough has been sacked 10 times. That’s not good for the offense, and it’s certainly not good to allow your starting quarterback to continue taking hits like that. The Saints will need to establish a running game around Shough on Monday night, and that challenge just got harder. Travis Etienne Jr. will miss some time after suffering a hamstring injury against the Raiders which means Kendre Miller and Alvin Kamara will become the focal points of the rushing attack. The Saints also did a great job utilizing their tight ends on Sunday, creating mismatches by incorporating more 12 personnel. Noah Fant and Juwan Johnson both played very well because of it. And, obviously, get the ball to Chris Olave. Olave is making a case to be the best receiver in the league right now, and the Saints need to continue featuring him in the offense. Find that Guardian Cap early and often on Monday night. Finally, encourage Shough to run. He has good mobility and can make a defense pay when its pass rushers become undisciplined. Encourage him to use his legs and make the defense think twice about sending blitzes. He can get rid of the ball quickly and extend plays with his feet. The Falcons have been able to generate pressure with just four rushers, so it will be important for Shough to make them pay whenever they decide to send more than that. The Matchup : When it comes to this matchup, the Saints have the advantage in talent at the quarterback position, while the Falcons have the advantage in the talent surrounding their quarterback. This is an important game because it’s a divisional matchup, and the Saints are coming off a loss. They can’t afford to lose games within the division if they want to have a chance at the postseason. The NFC South isn’t a particularly strong division, so the Saints need to come out and win. To do that, they must make sure they showcase that they have the better quarterback on the field Monday night. Who do you think has the advantage heading into this matchup, and how do you think this game will turn out?

summary: The New Orleans Saints are honoring the 20th anniversary of their iconic Domecoming game with another Monday Night Football matchup against the Atlanta Falcons. The Domecoming game is the one of most emotional and significant moments in Saints history, and Monday is simply a game New Orleans needs to win. On top of being an […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - SEPTEMBER 27: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints throws a pass against the Las Vegas Raiders during the first half of an NFL game on September 27. 2026, at Caesars Superdome in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are honoring the 20th anniversary of their iconic Domecoming game with another Monday Night Football matchup against the Atlanta Falcons. The Domecoming game is the one of most emotional and significant moments in Saints history, and Monday is simply a game New Orleans needs to win. On top of being an NFC South matchup, the Domecoming reunion could either kick-start a big run for the Saints, or be the game we point to when it all goes wrong. The Saints need to take advantage of these pivotal matchups to come away with a win on Monday. Saints run defense vs. RB Bijan Robinson The strength of the Falcons is clearly superstar running back Bijan Robinson. The fourth-year running back has been unstoppable since entering the league and is at the peak of his prime. While Robinson is one of the premier players in the NFL, the Falcons’ offense is significantly lacking. Part of the Falcons ‘ shortcomings is their lack of talent at quarterback. Despite Michael Penix Jr. having a solid day in the upset win over the Green Bay Packers, the way to stop Atlanta is slowing down Robinson. The Falcons have the second-best rushing offense in the league and a favorable matchup against the Saints’ run defense, which is ranked the sixth-worst in the NFL. Slowing down Robinson will be difficult, but will prove to be worthwhile, forcing Atlanta’s bottom-five passing offense to beat them in the air. Saints RBs vs. Falcons run defense Running back Travis Etienne Jr. finally started to look promising after a slow start to the season, but left during the team’s Week 3 loss with a hamstring injury. After further testing, it was determined Etienne’s injury was significant enough, and he was placed on injured reserve. With Etienne out, the offense looks towards veterans Alvin Kamara and Kendre Miller. The Saints’ run offense has been awful this season. Tyler Shough has been forced to throw 132 passes through three games, and it has not been sustainable. On top of his 132 pass attempts, the lack of a run game has allowed teams to blitz Shough at a high rate. Part of the Saints’ failures to run the ball has been the poor play design. New Orleans’ run game isn’t creative and doesn’t utilize their backs’ strengths. Kellen Moore clearly knows what it’s like to run a successful rushing offense, but it has not followed him to New Orleans. But getting the run game going on Monday will be the Saints’ offense’s strongest matchup yet. Surprisingly, the Falcons have the best run defense in the NFL, allowing just 47.7 rushing yards per game. QB Tyler Shough vs. Falcons secondary Tyler Shough had a career game against the Las Vegas Raiders, and it would look a lot better if you just turned a blind eye to what happened in the fourth quarter. Obviously, however, the fourth-quarter meltdown can’t be ignored. But Shough may be in for another career day against Atlanta. While they house the best run defense in the NFL, the Falcons also have the fourth-worst passing defense and are now without their star cornerback, A.J. Terrell Jr. With Chris Olave’s big season continuing and Shough coming off a big day, New Orleans could take advantage of a favorable matchup.

title: Survey results: NY Giants fans think they’ll see J.J. McCarthy soon
summary: It wasn’t a surprise that the New York Giants brought in another quarterback once it was confirmed that Jaxson Dart was lost for the season. No disrespect to Jake Haener, but the Giants couldn’t go through a season with him as their primary backup quarterback — nor go through a season with just two quarterbacks […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants quarterbacks J.J. McCarthy (left) and Jaxson Dart (right) | Getty Images It wasn’t a surprise that the New York Giants brought in another quarterback once it was confirmed that Jaxson Dart was lost for the season. No disrespect to Jake Haener, but the Giants couldn’t go through a season with him as their primary backup quarterback — nor go through a season with just two quarterbacks in the building. It was a surprise, however, that the Giants relinquished draft capital for a quarterback, and that the quarterback was former Minnesota Vikings 10th overall pick J.J. McCarthy. The trade has been controversial, with some fans approving strongly while others decrying the move for McCarthy. Overall, however, most Giants seem to think trading a 5th round pick for the former 10th overall pick is a good — but not great — move. The splash created by the trade aside, Jameis Winston is still the Giants’ starting quarterback. Head Coach John Harbaugh confirmed that this week, saying that Winston would be the starter for as long as he could foresee. Of course, life comes at you fast in the NFL, and while the Giants won their first game with Winston as the starter, his play wasn’t exactly inspiring. That’s left room for doubt as to how far into the future Harbaugh is actually forecasting. So we asked Giants’ fans how long they think it’ll be until McCarthy takes over for Winston as the Giants’ starter. The most common response was “about as soon as possible”, with the runner up being “once he learns the offense.” It’s worth noting that McCarthy is only just learning the Giants’ offense at this point. The Giants are in the process of teaching him the foundations of their offense and will move on to teaching the rest as the weeks progress. That’s going to be a process, and while the offense is somewhat similar to what he ran in Michigan under Jim Harbaugh, it’s still much more sophisticated. Jameis Winston doing just enough for the Giants to win last week hasn’t inspired much confidence that he can be the Giants’ starter through the remainder of the season. The other factor driving the speculation that McCarthy will take over sooner rather than later is his athleticism. While the quarterback run game wasn’t exactly a featured component of the offense with Jaxson Dart — the Giants weren’t running a Georgia Tech or Academy style triple option — the threat of the run was an important weapon. It’s a weapon that Winston doesn’t really possess, and the loss of that potential for a quarterback run changed how the Giants have to scheme their offense. We only have a one game sample size, but the early returns were discouraging, and the Giants’ red zone offense was notably different (and bad). The thinking seems to be that while McCarthy doesn’t have Dart’s accuracy and touch as a passer, he does combine a strong arm with impressive movement skills. The Giants have a non-traditional collection of skill position players with just three pure receivers, four running backs, a hybrid tight end, three traditional tight ends, and a fullback. We saw against the Dallas Cowboys that it can be effective in attacking defenses in ways they aren’t commonly built to handle. However, the question is whether a traditional pocket passer like Jameis Winston can get the most out of those skill position players — in addition to the questions as to how much Winston has left. It’s possible that the Giants won’t be able to effectively “change lanes” as Matt Nagy put it, and might need a mobile quarterback to slow the defense and create opportunities for the unconventional skill position players. As things stand now, the Giants are 2.5-point underdogs against the Arizona Cardinals at home, per FanDuel . There’s an opportunity there for Winston to prove his doubters wrong and for the Giants to start building momentum. Right now, however, it’s notable that fan confidence has rebounded after the Giants’ win over the Titans. Winning makes everything better, though some fans reacted to the Giants’ win over the Titans as though it was a loss. It’s true that the Giants very nearly lost a game they should have dominated against the Titans. However, there’s also something to be said for remaining resilient and finding ways to win even when you’re your own worst enemy. That win, and perhaps the trade for McCarthy, seems to have heartened Giants’ fans despite losing Brian Burns for the year to a torn ACL. Multiple Giants veterans admitted that the team would likely have lost that same game a year ago. We’ll just have to see if the team is able to use it as a stepping stone as they forge a path forward without Jaxson Dart and Brian Burns. If they’re able to do so, we’ll see fan confidence continue to rise.

title: NFL Week 4 betting advice: Giants-Cards picks and props
summary: Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 4 edition! Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that are less than -120. No gimmes! The Giants are 2-1, after narrowly escaping against the lowly Titans in the wind […]
full_text: Game! | Getty Images Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 4 edition! Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that are less than -120. No gimmes! The Giants are 2-1, after narrowly escaping against the lowly Titans in the wind and rain last Sunday. The good news is they get to stay at home for another game against one of the league’s weaker teams. The Arizona Cardinals are this week’s visitors, and they come in 1-2 after losing a 36-30 shootout in San Francisco last Sunday. Her’s one way to look at this stretch of New York’s schedule – Big Blue had the fifth pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, and their Week 3 and 4 opponents – both at home – are two of the teams that picked ahead of them. You’d think the Giants would be favored this week, and before the season began, that was correct. But that was then, and this is now, and the devastating Jaxson Dart injury changed everything. Throw in last week’s season-ending injury to the Giants’ best player on the other side of the ball (Brian Burns), and our boys are underdogs, at home, to a team that came into this season with the second lowest projected win total in the league. The Cardinals have been frisky, and better than advertised. They started their season with a big road upset over the Chargers, before predictably losing to two of the three powerhouses in their division. There’s no shame in losing to the Seahawks and 49ers, and they’re no pushover. Unlike Tennessee, they’ve got some very dangerous weapons on offense, which could cause problems for Dennard Wilson’s depleted defense. This game is one respite in what is truly a brutal stretch of their schedule. I had a very nice 3-0 sweep with my column picks last week (woo-hoo!) and will try to stay hot this week. I had a lot of trouble making my game pick for the Staff picks column, so I’m staying away from the line. Let’s get to this week’s picks. All lines and odds are from Fanduel and are as of Friday, October 2. The forecast for Sunday is cloudy and comfortable, with a slight chance of light rain. After last week, I don’t think anyone will mind a little drizzle. The line for the game is Cardinals -2.5, with a game total of 43.5. Game total OVER 43.5 (-118) . This total feels low to me. The Giants have played it very conservative in Jameis Winston’s first two games, and the result has been just one interception, but also zero touchdowns in 20 drives. You can chalk some of that up to the circumstances of the first game and the weather in the second. They’re going to need to score in the 20s (at least) to win this game and I think you’ll see a more aggressive game plan. On the other side of the ball, Arizona has several players who can move the chains and make big plays, and I won’t be surprised if this is a mini-shootout. Both teams have notable injuries on defense. 43.5 is a relatively low total – grab it. Jeremiyah Love most rushing yards in the game (-110). The Cardinals got roasted for taking a running back with the third pick in the 2026 draft. We’ll never know if the G-Men would’ve taken him if he fell to pick five. After recovering from an ankle injury suffered in the first preseason game, Love is beginning to assert himself. After seeing just 20 carries across the first two games, he got 21 last week, to just two for running mate Tyler Allgeier. Coach Mike LaFleur cited a “hot hand” approach, but they didn’t use a Top-3 pick on Love to keep him in the garage. The QBs are old and don’t run much, so to hit this prop Love basically just has to outgain Cam Skattebo, who is splitting the work with two other backs. I like those odds. Michael Wilson OVER 57.5 receiving yards (-114). Wilson saw 17 targets last week. Sounds like an outlier game, right? It’s not. He was targeted ten or more times in five of Jacoby Brissett’s starts last season, and at least seven times in all but one of Arizona’s final nine games last season. The Giants’ pass rush and secondary are depleted, and it was troubling to see Cam Ward picking them apart on the final two drives last Sunday, in terrible weather. Brissett should have success finding his favorite targets and that includes Wilson. Those are the picks for Week 4. Good luck with your wagers! And if you play fantasy football, be sure to check out my Week 4 fantasy preview, with start/sit advice and more, right here .
