title: Eagles thoughts: Course corrections
summary: The Eagles are an uninspiring 2-1. The Rams are a disappointing 1-2. Someone is going to walk away on Sunday feeling somewhat less bad about themselves. Football is not a meritocracy  Before the season began I asked if the new Sean Mannion led offense would get complimentary players more involved. We got our first look […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - SEPTEMBER 27: Head coach Sean McVay of the Los Angeles Rams looks on during the first quarter against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field At Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Tafoya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles are an uninspiring 2-1. The Rams are a disappointing 1-2. Someone is going to walk away on Sunday feeling somewhat less bad about themselves. Football is not a meritocracy Before the season began I asked if the new Sean Mannion led offense would get complimentary players more involved . We got our first look at an answer on Monday with a stark result: no, not even a little. Against the Titans, Darius Cooper had a nice catch and run for 23 yards on 1st and 17, and later scored the game winning TD. He’s been outstanding on special teams. The head coach likes him. His reward? 4 snaps on offense against the Bears, fewer than Elijah Moore. Meanwhile Makai Lemon played 35, a season high 70%. Tank Bigsby was the only skill position player to play fewer snaps than Cooper. Will Shipley, EJ Jenkins, and Johnny Mundt all played double digit snaps on both special teams and offense. Cooper did so against the Titans. Now with DeVonta Smith set to miss a few games, Cooper should get the chance on offense he deserves. There is no excuse not to. The red flag of yellow flags In my preview of the Rams, I noted that they had the best penalty differential in 2025 , which was unlikely to repeat itself in 2026. The Eagles, coincidentally, had the worst. Through three games the Rams have most definitely not repeated their success: they have the worst penalty differential, with -13 total penalties and -105 penalty yards. The Eagles are 18th. Half of the Rams penalties were last week against the Broncos, but in each of their first two games they had double the amount of their opponent, so this wasn’t just a one week thing. There’s no guarantee that this trend will continue, if anything they’re due for a game where they have a positive differential, but it is one reason among several why they’re 1-2 to start their supposed dream season. Lies, damn lies, and statistics Nick Sirianni has never lost to Sean McVay, going 4-0 against him. Since Sirianni became a head coach, he’s been more successful than McVay: Wins: Eagles 2nd, Rams 10th Points: Eagles 6th, Rams 9th Yards: Eagles 7th, Rams 9th Super Bowl appearances: Eagles 2, Rams 1 Super Bowl wins: Eagles 1, Rams 1 College Football Watch List 12:00 – Alabama at Mississippi State The 2027 QB draft class is so predictably disappointing that people are already on to the 2028 class, which is was also extremely predictable. Mississippi State QB Kamario Taylor is already high on next year’s radar. Bulldogs RB Fluff Bothwell (not his real name) is a dual threat RB making a name for himself. Alabama QB Keelon Russell is also on next year’s radar (neither he nor Taylor are draft eligible this year). For this year safety Bray Hubbard is fun, a big hitter who can make plays, 8 INTs and 4 FFs. 3:30 – Ohio State at Iowa and Florida at Missouri You are not going to believe this but Iowa has some OL, TE, and safety prospects. Shocker, I know. All three are Eagles needs! RG Kade Pieper is one of the top interior lineman prospects, and LT Trevor Lauck one of the top OT prospects. At 6’5” Lauck is smaller than teams, especially the Eagles. traditionally like in OTs. Pieper has experience at center.

title: Steelers news: Grading the Joey Porter Jr. trade
summary: After months of a contract saga that slowly looked worse and worse for the Steelers, cornerback Joey Porter Jr. was traded to the Cowboys less than 24 hours before Pittsburgh’s Week 4 matchup against the Cleveland Browns. The outcome was’t unsurprising following Porter’s lack of participation with the team throughout the offseason and during the […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - NOVEMBER 30: Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. (24) looks on during the NFL football game between the Buffalo Bills and Pittsburgh Steelers on November 30, 2025 at Acrisure Stadium in Pittsburgh, PA. (Photo by Mark Alberti/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After months of a contract saga that slowly looked worse and worse for the Steelers, cornerback Joey Porter Jr. was traded to the Cowboys less than 24 hours before Pittsburgh’s Week 4 matchup against the Cleveland Browns. The outcome was’t unsurprising following Porter’s lack of participation with the team throughout the offseason and during the first few weeks of regular season play. He was often listed as having a back injury, but by the end it seemed obvious that it was a cover for a contract holdout of sorts. The cornerback market skyrocketed in value this offseason, and Porter was undoubtedly looking for a hefty payday following his breakout 2025 campaign — and he still might not get that deal from the Cowboys, who notably did not have an extension agreement in place when they traded for Porter. Still, the Steelers are now without a promising cornerback in a year where the team clearly should be trying to collect a strong foundation of young players — and Pittsburgh looks thin when it comes to talent in the secondary, as well. Was the 2028 second-round pick and conditional 2027 sixth really a fair price to get in return? At face value, this didn’t look like a great trade for the Steelers. full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers’ secondary was seen as a very deep unit heading into the season. However, following the Joey Porter Jr trade and an ankle injury to Jamel Dean, the Steelers suddenly have a need at cornerback after Daylen Everette was torched on Thursday. A trade for a notable name would be nice, but the likelier outcome is a free agent signing. There are multiple notable names available that would make sense, and here are a few of my favorites. Kyu Blu Kelly Kelly is already an NFL journeyman just three years into his career. After spending 2023 with three teams, Kelly spent 2024 and 2025 with the Las Vegas Raiders under defensive coordinator Patrick Graham, and had a solid 2025 season that saw him pick off three passes in 13 games. At minimum, he knows the defense and would be better than Everette was against Cleveland. He did suffer a season-ending knee injury last December, which is a large reason he is still available. Marshon Lattimore Lattimore didn’t have the best run with the Washington Commanders, but he was largely solid in zone coverage last season. He broke up three passes and allowed less than a yard per coverage snap when the Commanders were in zone, per Sumer Sports. The only pushback here would be Lattimore’s age, as he is 30 years old. Tre’Davious White Again, White is on the older side at 31 years of age. But like Lattimore, he was good in zone looks last year. Anytime you see these former high-end corners age, they usually are still good in zone looks due to their high football IQs. In 275 coverage snaps, White allowed 16 receptions as the nearest defender and 0.64 yards per coverage snap. with six pass breakups and an interception. Let us know what you think in the comments . full_text: (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images Midway through the 2026 preseason, the Pittsburgh Steelers made the very popular decision to bring back linebacker Elandon Roberts. The Steelers’ linebacking corps was in need of a true thumper and run-stopper, and there was a spot for Roberts to slot in as a big part of the rotation. Instead, the Steelers surprisingly released Roberts during final roster cuts, meaning they made no additions to the room from a season ago. In Thursday night’s loss to the Cleveland Browns, it was clear that they could have used No. 50. Per Mina Kimes, the Steelers allowed 108 yards on missed tackles against Cleveland. It wasn’t a great night for Patrick Queen or Payton Wilson, but especially Wilson. Per Sumer Sports , Wilson was credited with three missed tackles and no run stops. That gives Wilson seven missed tackles on the season, which leads the NFL. Queen has four on the year, and led the league in missed tackles a season ago. The Browns took advantage of Pittsburgh’s poor tackling, and it was a massive difference-maker in the game, especially on Cleveland’s first score that saw running back Jaleel McLaughlin break multiple tackles on his way to the end zone. Moving on from Roberts is just another poor roster decision for the Steelers that unfortunately continue to stack up. They should amend their mistake and bring Roberts back to put in the middle of their defense. Let us know what you think in the comments . full_text: The Seattle Seahawks play the entire AFC West this season, throwing it back to the days when they were in the division from 1977-2001. Their first AFC West opponent will be the Los Angeles Chargers, who are 0-3 and banged up, but not to be taken lightly. It’s also the first time Jim Harbaugh will play the Seahawks in a meaningful game without Pete Carroll on the sidelines since he quarterbacked an eventual 1-15 San Diego Chargers squad to a 17-15 loss at Husky Stadium in 2000. CBS will have the 1:25 pm PT broadcast of this game, and it is a distant third in terms of game distribution and, frankly, interest. The Kansas City Chiefs and Las Vegas Raiders are the main game, while the Denver Broncos and San Francisoc 49ers are the secondary game. Not even Alaska or Hawaii will be getting this one, so your best bet to get Seahawks vs. Chargers on your local CBS affiliate is to live in Washington, Oregon, Western Idaho, a sliver of Western Montana, or the Los Angeles and San Diego regions. Check to see if you’re in the 506 Sports green zone. Calling the game will be Andrew Catalon and former New England Patriots safety Logan Ryan, who won two Super Bowls with the Patriots but lost a Super Bowl with the San Francisco 49ers, as is the usual thing the 49ers have done in Super Bowls this century. Seahawks fans have heard Catalon’s voice a few times, including last year’s 44-13 win over the New Orleans Saints, the 2024 loss to the New York Giants, and a couple of games in 2023. Seattle will either be the featured game (Week 5 vs. San Francisco 49ers) or nationally televised (Weeks 6-8 at Denver Broncos, vs. Kansas City Chiefs, vs. Chicago Bears) over the next month, so the Seahawks will be seen by a much larger audience very soon. Check out 506 Sports for the remaining game announcers and TV maps.

title: Seahawks’ DeMarcus Lawrence, Brady Russell fined following loss to Commanders
summary: The Seattle Seahawks suffered their first loss of the season in a 33-31 upset against the Washington Commanders, and there’s now some money that will be lost by a couple of veteran players for their actions during the game. DeMarcus Lawrence, who’s no stranger to playing the Commanders after a long career with the Dallas […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks suffered their first loss of the season in a 33-31 upset against the Washington Commanders, and there’s now some money that will be lost by a couple of veteran players for their actions during the game. DeMarcus Lawrence, who’s no stranger to playing the Commanders after a long career with the Dallas Cowboys, was extremely fortunate to get away with roughing the passer against Marcus Mariota late in the second quarter. Mariota completed a pass to Terry McLaurin after getting whacked in the face by Lawrence. No penalty was called, but the league still fined Lawrence $17,111 for an illegal hit on the quarterback. Special teams ace and fullback/H-back Brady Russell was also fined for an uncalled penalty in the same quarter. On a Michael Dickson punt, Russell can be seen running over Commanders tight end Colston Yankoff (No. 80) after the ball was fair caught. That will cost Russell $11,111 for an “away from the play” violation. Two Seahawks were fined after the Commanders game. DeMarcus Lawrence was docked $17,911 for an uncalled roughing the passer (blow to the head/neck). Brady Russell was fined $11,111 for an "away from the play" hit on Colston Yankoff on what was otherwise a fair caught punt. pic.twitter.com/qV9EiarzSd — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) October 3, 2026 Can’t really argue too much with either of those decisions. The TV broadcast made it clear that Lawrence got away with a helmet shot, whereas the All-22 of Russell’s infraction is clear-cut. Neither of these offenses will count toward a possible one-game suspension based on the new rules . And lest anyone think that Michael Dickson got roughed, his kicking leg returned to the ground and the contact was not deemed severe enough to warrant a flag. There were no fines for any Commanders players.

title: 5Qs and 5As, Seahawks vs. Chargers preview: What’s wrong with Jim Harbaugh’s team?
summary: The Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Chargers looked like a fascinating game when the schedule was released in May. You have the reigning Super Bowl champions going against a Jim Harbaugh team led by quarterback Justin Herbert. Former Miami Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel was brought in to elevate Herbert and the offense to top-tier […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Chargers looked like a fascinating game when the schedule was released in May. You have the reigning Super Bowl champions going against a Jim Harbaugh team led by quarterback Justin Herbert. Former Miami Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel was brought in to elevate Herbert and the offense to top-tier status, much in the way he transformed the Dolphins offense in his first couple of seasons with Tua Tagovailoa. The Chargers were a playoff team in each of the past two seasons, albeit without any wins, and expectations were high to take that next step. There will be no playoffs for the Chargers unless they turn things around drastically. An 0-3 start has seen the Chargers score just 46 points total, with the usual set of injuries impacting the Chargers roster. To preview Seahawks-Chargers, I asked Bolts From The Blue’s Michael Peterson to give us a better understanding of the Chargers’ disastrous start to the season, as well as players to watch on Sunday. Let’s get to 5 Qs and 5 As! 1.) The Chargers offense was supposed to be a force under new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel. The offense is a disaster and they’ve yet to score more than 16 points. How much are you putting on McDaniel’s scheme, and do you think this roster is well equipped to run the offense McDaniel wants? I think it’s difficult not to put the majority of the blame on McDaniel given that it’s his own system and he had the ability to pick and choose some of the players the Chargers added this offseason (Guard Cole Strange and running back Keaton Mitchell in free agency, wide receiver Brenen Thompson in the draft). He only further incurs more of the blame since the signing of Strange to be the unquestioned starter at right guard due to his experience (NOT success) in the system was seen as a horrendous decision well before now. Other than that, I thought the likes of Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnston would be great in this system as long as McDaniel used them both in roles that suited their skillsets best. McConkey worked out! Johnston, on the other hand, has not. I would, however, be remiss not to mention that tight ends are important in this offense and the Chargers have been without their tpop two guys for roughly a game and a half this year. They haven’t been healthy enough to truly get everyone on the same page and are now forced to do it with backups and players who otherwise shouldn’t ever be on the field. Lastly with McDaniel, the buck stops with him in regards to his unit. If the whole dang offense looks like they’ve never played together, that’s an issue! What was being down for six months prior to the season? Justin Herbert looks nothing like the guy we all came to know. Why is the system making every good player look much worse? We have so many questions. General manager Joe Hortiz also deserves some blame for a very questionable offseason where they had all the money in the world to build this team and he went with numerous bargain-bin deals instead. 2.) A lot of the scrutiny surrounding the Chargers is about the play of Justin Herbert. He’s been victimized by another poor offensive line, brutal drops by his receivers, and not much of a running game. But when I look at the Bills game, Herbert looked pretty fortunate to only throw one interception with some of his questionable decisions. How do you think Herbert has performed thus far, and how much of the offensive struggles can be attributed to him? If I really had to put a number on how much of a role Herbert has played in the offense’s struggles, I’d put it around 30%. He still has made a number of plays that make you go “oh, that’s the good stuff I remember” but that’s contrasted to far too many questionable decisions, as well. The anticipation that McDaniel wants Herbert to throw with does NOT look like it jives with him. The film shows me over and over again that Herbert wants to fully see his guys open before throwing and that’s not what the system needs. That’s where the lack of trust between him and his receivers shows the brightest. He does NOT want to throw as early as he needs to and he’s leaving a lot of yards out there.” One of the strangest habits of Herbert this year so far has got to be his complete evasion from throwing the checkdowns. I mean, it’s actually wild how many times they could have moved the chains for put themselves in favorable situations if he would have just made the easy, less-sexy throw. He has stayed so locked on to his guys down the field that third and fourth options don’t seem to register with him anymore. It’s concerning! 3.) The Chargers lost Jesse Minter to the Baltimore Ravens, and Minter was held in high regard for how the Chargers defense performed over his two seasons as defensive coordinator. Chris O’Leary is in charge of the defense and thus far the results have been middling. However, they did force five turnovers against the Bills, so there have been positive signs. What’s your assessment of the Chargers defense under O’Leary? I believe Chris O’Leary will ultimately be fine with more time under his belt as a NFL coordinator. The first game or two showed us the lumps he needed to take, but the Bills game was seemingly him settling down and finding a groove against one of the best offenses in the NFL. He does it his own way with dialing up pressure but overall has stayed fairly close to what Minter did while he was in charge. They want to keep things in front of them and play a lot of zone. Make the opposing offense win over and over again to go the length of the field. Do not let them get easy yards and chunk plays. This week will be another difficult task, but I have confidence the defense will hold their own this week once again. 4.) Who are some names to look out for on offense and defense who aren’t the superstars? In other words, some under-the-radar talents instead of Herbert, Ladd McConkey, Khalil Mack, and Derwin James. On offense, second-year wideout Tre’ Harris has seemingly grabbed the WR2 job behind McConkey. He has shown sure hands and will block his tail off. When the Chargers have needed big plays the last two weeks, he’s been able to author them. Defensively, Justin Eboigbe has been a standout guy. He had six sacks in 2025 and that was huge given that he barely made the roster as a rookie who suffered from being a ‘tweener at Alabama. He now has a knack for being around the football and will make several splash plays per game. He’s a very underrated player on the Chargers defense right now. 5.) Do you think the Chargers can possibly salvage their season and pull off the upset in Seattle? And if this season is a complete bust, what does the future hold for Jim Harbaugh and general manager Joe Hortiz? I personally do not think the Chargers will win this week, nor any week prior to their Week Seven bye. I just can’t. That’s how bad and discombobulated this offense has looked and they are not the type of problems that simply get better overnight or in the span of several weeks. I think they may keep ot close this week thanks to the defense, but there’s no way the offense does enough this week against the league’s best defense. As far as the future, a year where they finish under .500 should mean that major changes are made. It SHOULD. But I don’t think the Chargers will do that. Harbaugh has earned the benefit of the doubt. He will stay at least one more year if this season is a travesty. The guy who I believe deserves far more blame is Hortiz whom I mentioned earlier. His draft history now looks questionable and his offensive free-agent history looks downright dreadful. The lack of urgency to fix the offensive line has been egregious and the guys they chose to save money on were more than likely way worse than they themselves would have ever expected. And to be completely fair, a lot of the best signings have been irrelevant due to injuries which is no one’s fault, but that doesn’t mean it’s any less frustrating because it…

title: John Schneider’s offseason decisions: Process, results, and the questions after 3 games
summary: John Schneider didn’t enter this offseason with a roster that needed to be rebuilt from the ground up. The Seahawks had just reached and won the Super Bowl. The job was to keep the team at that level. Three games into the season, some of those decisions are starting to raise questions. But there’s an […]
full_text: John Schneider didn’t enter this offseason with a roster that needed to be rebuilt from the ground up. The Seahawks had just reached and won the Super Bowl . The job was to keep the team at that level. Three games into the season, some of those decisions are starting to raise questions. But there’s an important distinction to make when evaluating an NFL offseason: judging a decision is not the same as judging its result. A good decision can produce a bad outcome. A questionable decision can work out. A general manager’s job isn’t to predict the future. It’s to make the best decision possible with the information available at the time, then adjust when new information arrives. That’s the framework for looking at Schneider’s offseason. This isn’t about handing out verdicts after three games. It’s about identifying which issues look like process problems and which may be the result of injuries, circumstances or bad luck. The $17 million Rashid Shaheed question Seattle gave Rashid Shaheed a three-year, $51 million extension with $34 million guaranteed — an average of $17 million per season. It’s natural to look at Kenneth Walker producing in Kansas City after signing a three-year, $43.05 million deal and wonder why Seattle didn’t use that money to keep its former running back. But that comparison, by itself, is too simplistic. Walker had durability concerns that played into Seattle’s decision. Tory Horton was also injured, which may have increased the perceived need for a player like Shaheed. The bigger question is what Seattle believed Shaheed could become. Shaheed is an explosive, dynamic player. His value as a returner and his ability to create big plays are real. In 15 games with the Seahawks, including the playoffs, Shaheed has just 24 receptions — 1.6 per game. Through three games this season, he has been targeted 12 times, catching six passes for 53 yards. Seven of those 12 targets traveled fewer than 10 yards, and Seattle is 0-for-1 on passes of 20-plus yards thrown his way. But he had never consistently shown that he could be a true WR2 even with Klint Kubiak. His biggest weapon is his speed, but that speed loses some of its value when Seattle isn’t using him to threaten defenses vertically. If the goal of the contract was to turn him into a WR2, that kind of usage needs to show up. His special teams production has also dropped. His punt-return average went from 16.2 yards in 2025 to 9.7 this season, although that is obviously still a three-game sample. That doesn’t mean the contract can already be called a mistake. Shaheed’s role can change, and the season is still young. But when you evaluate the process, there is a legitimate question: What did Seattle see in Shaheed’s history that justified paying $17 million per year with the expectation that he could become a WR2? KaVontae Turpin provides some useful context. The Cowboys returner signed a three-year deal that can reach $18 million, or up to $6 million per year. Turpin isn’t a perfect comparison because the players have different roles. But Seattle didn’t pay Shaheed $17 million per year simply to be a great returner. They paid him expecting him to provide meaningful value as a receiver, too. That’s the expectation that needs to be evaluated. Kenneth Walker and the danger of hindsight It’s easy to look at what Kenneth Walker is doing in Kansas City and decide Seattle should have simply kept him. But that would mean evaluating the decision entirely through its current result. Walker’s talent was never really the question. The concern was whether he could stay healthy and consistently handle a larger workload. Seattle managed his usage at different points, and sharing the backfield was part of the roster construction. Now, in Kansas City, Walker is getting more responsibility and producing. If he stays healthy throughout the season, Seattle’s decision will naturally look different. But Schneider couldn’t know that during the offseason. That’s why it doesn’t make much sense to simply compare Shaheed’s $17 million per year to Walker’s roughly $14.35 million and argue that Seattle should have given one contract instead of the other. The point is that the result can’t be used to rewrite the process. The bigger problem in the backfield Seattle selected Jadarian Price with the 32nd overall pick . Price has talent and could develop into a very good player. The question was always how prepared he was to immediately become the Seahawks’ RB1. He wasn’t coming off a history of being an established full-time starter. The pick was heavily based on what Seattle believed he could become. That could work. The problem was the lack of a safety net behind him. During the offseason, Seattle didn’t even know exactly when Zach Charbonnet would be available. That created a very real possibility that Price would have to carry the backfield immediately. The alternatives were George Holani and Emanuel Wilson. Neither had a track record that gave Seattle the same level of confidence as an experienced back capable of handling a significant workload. There were ways to lower that risk. Tyler Allgeier signed with the Cardinals, while Rachaad White was another veteran option available in free agency. Neither would have guaranteed a solution, and I’m not arguing that Seattle needed to sign either one. But both had experience handling significant workloads in the NFL — something Wilson and Holani didn’t have. And that’s the important distinction: the problem wasn’t necessarily selecting Price. It was entering the season without a more proven option behind him if he wasn’t ready. Three games into the season, his ball-security issues have made that concern more obvious. Price already has two fumbles and lost playing time during the loss to Washington. There is still plenty of time to change that story. Charbonnet could return, Price could improve (once he returns from his own injury), and the problem could disappear. The same issue shows up at cornerback Seattle’s decision not to re-sign Riq Woolen and instead bring back Josh Jobe isn’t necessarily the biggest problem. Jobe improved under Mike Macdonald, so keeping him made sense. Woolen, meanwhile, may have received an offer Seattle didn’t believe fit its plans. The bigger issue is the depth behind Jobe. Jobe still needed to prove he could handle a larger role. Third-round pick Julian Neal was still developing. Trevon Diggs wasn’t ready to immediately take on a major role, while other options came with their own questions. Nehemiah Pritchett, who had been inconsistent in previous opportunities, has shown some better moments early this season. But once again, the same roster-building principle appears. When you enter a season relying on internal development that hasn’t happened yet, you increase the risk, and opposing offenses will naturally look for that weakness. That doesn’t mean Jobe can’t be a long-term starting corner. The point is that Seattle could have entered the season with more margin for error at the position. When the process makes sense Safety is a good example of why process and results have to be evaluated separately. Seattle lost Coby Bryant and selected Bud Clark in the second round. Clark had experience, versatility and the playmaking traits that made him a natural candidate to fill part of the role Bryant left behind. Then he got hurt . The result was bad, but that doesn’t automatically make the decision bad. If Seattle identified a need after losing Bryant and believed Clark could fill it, the process can still make sense even if an injury prevented the plan from working. The same principle applies, on a smaller scale, to Dante Fowler. Seattle didn’t draft an edge rusher to replace Boye Mafe. Instead, the team brought in Fowler as a relatively low-cost bet with a history of production. Through three games, he hasn’t provided the impact Seattle hoped for. But there’s a difference between a low-cost bet not working and a $17 million-per-year investment…

title: SBNation Reacts Results: Nearly 75 percent of Seahawks fans expect winning October
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Each week we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seattle Seahawks fans and fans across the country. The Seattle Seahawks suffered their first loss of the 2026 season last week…a big surprise considering they were facing the Washington Commanders. The main question in […]
full_text: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Each week we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seattle Seahawks fans and fans across the country. The Seattle Seahawks suffered their first loss of the 2026 season last week…a big surprise considering they were facing the Washington Commanders. The main question in this week’s poll asked how many games the Seahawks would win in October. The majority of you think the Seahawks will win three or four games this month even though the level of competition will see a notable uptick. After the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 4, Seattle will face the San Francisco 49ers, Denver Broncos, and Kansas City Chiefs. That’s a pretty wicked gauntlet for those last three games. In line with the win expectations for October, fan confidence is still riding high despite last week’s loss with 86% of fans feeling confident that the team is headed in the right direction. Last week was definitely a kick to the groin, but had the Seahawks not turned the ball over three times while not getting a turnover themselves, they probably win that game relatively easily. However, the reality is that they lost to an inferior team and can’t take the winless Los Angeles Chargers lightly. Maybe we should think of October as a “Former AFC West Rivalry” month since the Seahawks face three of the four teams in their former division. Add in the fact that the games against Denver and Kansas City are both prime time affairs, and we’ve got a pretty fun (and pivotal) month ahead. Oh yeah, and the Broncos game is featuring double throwback jerseys to add even more nostalgia to the affair. If the win total matches fan expectations, this will be an exciting month! full_text: The Seattle Seahawks will need veteran leadership to right their ship in Week 4 after a loss to the Washington Commanders, at least according to the team’s captains, which were announced on Friday. Seattle announced that Cooper Kupp, Mike Morris, Nehemiah Pritchett and former Los Angeles Charger Uchenna Nwosu will have the honors of being captains on Sunday. Between the four of them, they represent 26 years of experience in the NFL, though the majority of that stems from Kupp (10) and Nwosu (9). This is every player’s first selection this season and marks the first time that Pritchett, who is stepping up to replace Riq Woolen at starting cornerback, has been named a captain. Pritchett had an interception in Week 1 and has anchored an injured secondary through three games. Our Week 4 captains. Read more » https://t.co/kiaCZk0LRL pic.twitter.com/LkktVFuCe4 — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) October 2, 2026 Nwosu being named captain is an obvious choice as he was a second-round pick by the Chargers in 2018 before signing with the Seahawks in 2022. In addition to the bit of gamesmanship, Nwosu has become a fan-favorite in Seattle after he propelled a terrible pass-rush in 2022 and became a key part of the “Dark Side” defense. Not to mention his hit on Drake Maye in the Super Bowl, which led to a game clinching interception. Kupp, the lone offensive representative, has the second most receiving yards of any Seahawks player. The Eastern Washington alum has proven that he still has juice left to squeeze this season after a decade in the league, recording an immaculate catch in Week 1 and being a reliable target in clutch moments. Lastly, Morris, who is repping the special teams, returned to the lineup last week against the Commanders. The Seahawks fifth-round pick has been a staple of the team’s defensive line rotation the last two seasons, recording two TFLs and 23 tackles in that time frame. These four will lead the Seahawks onto the field as they face the winless Chargers at Lumen Field on Sunday at 1:25 p.m.

title: Colin Kaepernick suggests the 49ers were tanking with Chip Kelly in 2016
summary: 2016 was a rough time to be a 49ers fan, with the team going 2-14 while dealing with a dysfunctional front office. Former 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick suggests the 49ers didn’t want to win anyway. Kaepernick’s memoir, “The Perilous Fight,” has been out for a couple of weeks and tells his perspective on growing up […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FL - NOVEMBER 27: San Francisco 49ers head coach Chip Kelly talks with San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick (7) before a play during the NFL football game between the San Francisco 49ers and the Miami Dolphins on November 27, 2016, at the Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, FL. The Miami Dolphins defeated the San Francisco 49ers by the score of 31-24. (Photo by Robin Alam/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images 2016 was a rough time to be a 49ers fan, with the team going 2-14 while dealing with a dysfunctional front office. Former 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick suggests the 49ers didn’t want to win anyway. Kaepernick’s memoir, “ The Perilous Fight ,” has been out for a couple of weeks and tells his perspective on growing up and playing both college and professional football. 49ers fans looking for stories from his time as the starting quarterback won’t be disappointed. We’ve talked about his relationship with general manager Trent Baalke and head coach Jim Harbaugh, but Kaepernick also shares his perspective playing for the coaches that followed Harbaugh: Jim Tomsula in 2015, whose regime Kaepernick called “a disaster,” and Chip Kelly in 2016. Kelly named Blaine Gabbert the starting quarterback over Kaepernick. On the surface, it may have seemed like Gabbert beat Kaepernick for the starting job. In reality, Kaepernick was still rehabbing and returning from injury. There were also reports of injury guarantees on Kaepernick’s contract that he eventually restructured to remove—something many (including Kaepernick) speculate was the real reason he stayed off the field. That’s all common knowledge; what is interesting is Kaepernick’s take on the 49ers in 2016: I should add that the Niners didn’t seem interested in winning football games. They appeared to be in full “tank” mode. They were calling Chip Kelly’s first season a “rebuilding” year, but in actuality they had no plan to go get the talent Coach Kelly wanted. Kaepernick used the wide receiver situation as an example. Saying the 49ers’ No. 1 wideout that year was “the number five or six receiver on a different team.” No names are given, but Jeremy Kerley led the team in catches and yards receiving in 2016. Many may think of Torrey Smith as the “designated” wide receiver. Either way, Kerley’s team-leading 516 yards in receiving that year should tell you just how bad the 49ers were. “The team didn’t get us another receiver,” Kaepernick wrote. “Despite having the money to do so, something like $40 million in salary cap space.” Publicly, the 49ers were rebuilding. Even then, it was clear Baalke’s seat was nuclear after the press conference following Tomsula’s sacking took place; 49ers owner Jed York said he told Baalke he was not satisfied with the state of this [the 49ers] team. Was the team tanking? It wouldn’t be surprising. The 49ers’ lack of spending in free agency both in 2015 and 2016 didn’t make sense then, and it doesn’t make sense now (though there were rumors that players didn’t want to go to the 49ers with all the issues). The same could have been said for the Chip Kelly hire. We’ve already mentioned the offense, but Kelly’s defense under Jim O’Neil was one of the worst in league (not team) history. While the hire was a head-scratcher to begin with, the 49ers didn’t help Kelly get into a position to succeed. Kelly might have been a bad coach no matter what happened, but he was put in a failing situation regardless. There’s a strange alternate reality of what would have happened if Kelly had stayed with the 49ers for another couple of years and the team only let go of Baalke at the end of the 2016 season. It’s doubtful Kelly’s system would have succeeded no matter what the 49ers would have done, but it’s definitely a weird twilight zone moment.

title: 49ers News: Let Brandin Cook(s)
summary: What will we learn about this team from this match-up? The Broncos are like a scaled-down version of some of the beasts they’d need to slay on their way to the Super Bowl. A legit defensive line (but not quite Seattle), an athletic quarterback (but not quite a peak Mahomes or Josh Allen), and a […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - JANUARY 17: Ja'Quan McMillian #29 of the Denver Broncos fights for the ball with Brandin Cooks #18 of the Buffalo Bills during overtime of an AFC Divisional Playoff game at Empower Field At Mile High on January 17, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images What will we learn about this team from this match-up? The Broncos are like a scaled-down version of some of the beasts they’d need to slay on their way to the Super Bowl. A legit defensive line (but not quite Seattle), an athletic quarterback (but not quite a peak Mahomes or Josh Allen), and a veteran coach on Kyle’s level (but not quite Andy Reid). This almost feels like the starting gun to the “real” season. Here are the things I will be looking for, beyond the box score, that can tell us a lot about this team… Can the 49ers handle a ferocious pass rush? It’s great that the offensive line hasn’t given up a sack. They haven’t faced a defensive line this good yet. Seattle next week will be even better. Connor Colby and the interior o-line have exceeded my expectations so far, but this isn’t Miami or Arizona. Can the 49ers keep exploiting linebackers in coverage without their best wide receivers? Mike Evans might not play. All due respect to Brandin Cooks, but they need big games out of their non-WR skill players like George Kittle, Christian McCaffrey, and even a little Kyle Jusczyzk. That’s always been the case but especially so against the “elite DB/vulnerable LB” combination that Denver has going. Can the 49ers establish the run? Kansas City provided the blueprint in Week 1 when they forced the Broncos to miss 26 tackles. Can they keep an athletic quarterback in the pocket…. without Nick Bosa? Bo Nix isn’t as good as Matt Stafford but he is the most athletic QB they’ve faced yet (that’s still a mid-tier or above passer). He’s maddenly inconsistent but can also win games on his own. How’s the secondary holding up? Jaylen Waddle is good to go, and Courtland Sutton is no slouch. I can see a world where the Broncos start slow and then start coming back because of coverage busts on the back end. It just takes one bad bust to breathe life into Bo Nix, who otherwise struggles when forced to step up in the pocket. Wait, is the 49ers O-line actually good? Broncos, Seahawks can help settle the debate (paywall) “Offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said the big red zone sack Broncos safety Talanoa Hufanga had against the Los Angeles Rams late in Denver’s win Sunday shows how efficient — and aggressive — defensive coordinator Vance Joseph’s unit can be. Hufanga, a former 49er, lined up to quarterback Matthew Stafford’s blind side at the last second and was unaccounted for as he came off the edge. “He knows when to call his shots,” Kubiak said of Joseph. “He knows when to be aggressive and come after the quarterback. That group’s been playing together for a while. And when they call those blitzes, they usually work.” Part of the 49ers’ winning formula so far this year is that they aren’t hurting themselves.” Five 49ers to watch as Brock Purdy leads charge to stay undefeated vs. Broncos “Defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa clearly is the main guy. The 49ers need another player or two to stand out among their nine-man rotation. Rookie Gracen Halton could be on the verge of a breakout. Halton, a fourth-round 2026 NFL Draft pick, will make his third start in a row. He has a couple of tackles for loss, and appears to be trending toward making more big plays.” 49ers add a rookie to the injury report; Dante Pettis hurt his calf “Evans will be a game-time decision with his rib injury. Shanahan compared his rib injury to Evans, saying, “he’s definitely a lot tougher than me. Hopefully, he’s got a shot.” Brandin Cooks will make his 49ers debut on Sunday.” 49ers vs. Broncos: The Standard’s 5 fast predictions (paywall) “Kawakami: Broncos 27, 49ers 26. This would be a disappointing way for the 49ers to go into next weekend’s clash in Seattle. But they’re probably due for a flat performance perhaps with some natural focus on the flight to the Northwest coming up. Also, any more Eddy Piñeiro extra-point misses could be huge in a close game.” Kyle Shanahan shares final updates ahead of 49ers-Broncos “When you’re talking to your team about an upcoming opponent, do you find yourself have to talk up the opponent more or do you want to build your team’s confidence or appropriate fear? How do you approach it? “All of the above. Depends where we’re at at the time, where the team’s at. It changes every week. You can have it come off a huge win and people question the team you’re playing. That happened to us in Week Two. A big win versus the Rams in Australia. Then people have us as huge favorites and stuff the next week versus Miami. I don’t try to talk people up because I don’t think people believe words. I think people believe what they see and I can’t talk people up unless I believe it. So, I usually try to find it in the tape and show people what people can be and what they need to be worried about. It’s something I usually do earlier in the week. I think that fear to fail or respect of people, however you want to word it, is what gets you to work a certain way. The whole goal is to work hard enough so you don’t feel that way, and to me, the goal is to not feel that way by Saturday night so you go into Sunday confident. And if you feel that way on Monday, I usually think you’re in trouble. You’ve got to earn that. It’s got to be real, and that’s through the work you do and the preparation. You prepare the right way if you respect an opponent and I believe we respect whoever we’re playing every week.”

title: Josh Harris: ‘I like the spear,’ as reports of Commanders logo change surface
summary: Commanders owner Josh Harris was having a blast on Saturday during a fan rally a day before their Sunday game against the Indianapolis Colts in London.   Harris got on top of the bar to speak to the enormous crowd of Commanders fans at the event. full_text: Commanders owner Josh Harris was having a blast on Saturday during a fan rally a day before their Sunday game against the Indianapolis Colts in London. Harris got on top of the bar to speak to the enormous crowd of Commanders fans at the event. He bought everyone there not one round of beers but two. He also addressed the media members on-site covering the game. The topic of the Commanders logo came up, following up a report on social media discussing Washington’s preference to add the spear and “W” to their permanent logo as early as 2027. Zach Cohen posted original report on X/twitter on Friday morning. EXCLUSIVE: Sources tell me the Washington Commanders are planning to change their primary logo for the 2027 season And that logo is a familiar one: the team’s new alternate W logo with a spear running through it, unveiled in April with their new black “Hail Raiser” uniform I’m… pic.twitter.com/QVmK2EDNpt — Zach Cohen (@ZachCohenFB) October 2, 2026 Here’s what Harris had to say about it. “I like the spear. What can I say?” Harris told reporters. “It brings everything together a little bit. title: Five Washington Commanders players vital to beating Colts in London
summary: The Commanders are battling to even their early-season record after the first four weeks, needing to do so in a home game across the Atlantic Ocean and while starting a backup quarterback.   That’s not quite as bad as it sounds, considering what has been a solid Commanders travel plan and the fact Marcus Mariota […]
full_text: The Commanders are battling to even their early-season record after the first four weeks, needing to do so in a home game across the Atlantic Ocean and while starting a backup quarterback. That’s not quite as bad as it sounds, considering what has been a solid Commanders travel plan and the fact Marcus Mariota is the next man up. Washington remains an underdog even against a fellow 1-2 Indianapolis Colts team that has also dealt with daunting schedule. This is a winnable matchup, with some encouraging signs from Washington’s previous victory that suggests the job can be done. While Jayden Daniels wasn’t deemed ready after a Week 2 left elbow dislocation, the Commanders are getting some key players back. This new Terry McLaurin hamstring issue – Commanders reporter Ben Standig says not expected to play – could be a complication Let’s discuss five Commanders players (not named Marcus Mariota) key to beating Indianapolis, getting back to .500 and building on the momentum from last week’s win over Seattle: RB Bill Croskey-Merritt The second-year pro is averaging 3.0 yards per carry, with a 40% rushing success rate thus far this season. That’s, well, not great. He had an explosive touchdown run taken off the board by penalty, but that doesn’t change his overall inefficiency to start the season despite him seemingly being a solid fit for David Blough’s system. Rachaad White (shoulder) being unavailable will magnify his Week 4 impact, with Croskey-Merritt needing to be a featured offensive element. This could be a get-right game, with the Colts allowing 129.4 yards per game to this point. He’s obviously got to secure the football first and then make moves with it, lest his carry counts drop once guys get healthy and new re-signing Austin Ekeler gets fully up to speed. WR Stefon Diggs McLaurin’s playing status will impact how vital veteran Stefon Diggs is to this game, but it could be huge with the team’s No. 1 pass catcher reportedly not expected to play. That puts Diggs officially into WR1 status if McLaurin in fact can’t go. The veteran has been a touchdown generator to this point, with three in as many games . His targets have been high though his yardage totals haven’t, though we could seen an uptick against a No. 30-ranked Colts pass defense that certainly doesn’t scare you. This game should be close, and Diggs has the clutch gene and an ability to get open on critical downs. LB Frankie Luvu The veteran interior linebacker started this season wearing the green dot as the on-field defensive signal caller. He was also named a team captain for the first time, but his leadership was lost to a groin injury during the first half of Week 1. He’s finally able to return at a crucial time, following Leo Chenal’s season-ending neck fracture . The Commanders need Luvu to be a steadying presence in the middle and maintain their stellar run defense on the inside. His intensity can be infectious, and his partnership with rapidly improving rookie Sonny Styles should be an asset to Washington defensive coordinator Daronte Jones’ ability to call exotic pressures. iOL Lucas Patrick The Commanders signed the veteran center on Sept 16 , and he has already found his way onto the field. He played center in Week 3, with Nick Allgretti shifted into Sam Cosmi’s place at right guard. Patrick fared well despite his position’s cerebral, pre-snap requirements, playing better that Allegretti had there to this point. Cosmi didn’t make the trip to London for Sunday’s game, so we’ll likely see that same alignment against the Colts. It will be key in dealing with standout Indianapolis defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and in helping the run game go. If Patrick continues to play well, the Commanders should leave him at center and admit the Allegretti experiment was a mistake. DL Javon Kinlaw Javon Kinlaw has been excellent so far this season despite being banged up over the first few weeks. While defensive line stats aren’t super revealing , trust us when we say Kinlaw has been active around the quarterback and integral to the run defense that has become Washington’s early defensive signature. Kinlaw and the defensive front must be on point against standout Colts running back Jonathan Taylor.

Commanders beat writer Ben Standig reported on Saturday that the injury happened during […]
full_text: The Washington Commanders could be without their WR1 on Sunday versus Indianapolis, as Terry McLaurin deals with a new hamstring injury. He showed up on the injury report Friday, and was listed as questionable for the game after being limited in practice. Commanders beat writer Ben Standig reported on Saturday that the injury happened during the Commanders home opener win over the Seahawks in Week 3. McLaurin was listed as a full participant the first two days of practice, but Wednesday was a walk-through. Here’s an excerpt from Standig’s Saturday reporting — you can read the full story here : McLaurin apparently tweaked his hamstring during last week’s win over the Seattle Seahawks. After participating in practices this week, he was listed as “limited” in Friday’s session with a hamstring injury, and “questionable” for Sunday at Hotspur Tottenham Stadium. No final decision has been made on the status of Washington’s long-time top target. Despite hope that McLaurin would be able to play, the Commanders appear to be leaning toward caution to avoid the hamstring injury turning into a multi-week situation. Standig reported on Friday that there was still hope that he could play in London against the Colts, but that tune has changed this morning, and it looks more likely that McLaurin sits against his hometown team. The Commanders kept seven receivers on their roster, so they will have options available, and the team is getting tight end Chig Okonkwo back after a two-game absence for a hamstring injury. Austin Ekeler also rejoined the team after not playing for over a year. Washington has already ruled out Jayden Daniels, Rachaad White, Sam Cosmi, and Nick Cross for Sunday’s international game. summary: The Daily Slop – 3 October 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Tyler Warren #84 of the Indianapolis Colts is tackled by George Karlaftis #56 of the Kansas City Chiefs during the fourth quarter at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 3 October 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Home looks a little different this week 🏟️ @EASTERNMOTORS | #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/RAGu5w90Dm — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) October 3, 2026 Articles Commanders.com Hail Mail: Stopping Indy’s tight end @ChillMonkey123: How do you think they will stop Tyler Warren? They have been struggling with TE’s a lot lately. I really appreciate this question, because most of the attention has been around stopping Jonathan Taylor. Warren is undoubtedly a talented player and is off to a good start with 89 yards and two touchdowns on 22 targets. To your points, tight ends have generally done well against the Commanders. They’ve given up four touchdowns to tight ends so far this season, and most of them have come on similar plays. I think there are a few ways to prevent Warren from having similar success, and it starts with putting pressure on Daniel Jones. The Colts are 27th in pass block win rate and have already given up six sacks to the Kansas City Chiefs, Houston Texans and Baltimore Ravens. Assuming the Commanders can perform against the run to a similar standard as they did in the previous three games, it’s going to put the ball in Jones’ hands more often, which hasn’t fared well for the Colts. He has five of the team’s six giveaways and had two fumbles recovered against the Texans. Warren can’t get the ball if Jones struggles, and I can see the Commanders’ pass rush really getting after him this weekend. I think there are some changes in coverage that could be beneficial for the Commanders as well. If Frankie Luvu does return this weekend, that could free up Sonny Styles to take on more responsibility in the passing game. Styles has proven himself as a quality cover linebacker that can handle his own against running backs and tight ends alike. He actually has the sixth-best cover grade for a linebacker through three games, according to Pro Football Focus. I could see the Commanders matching Warren’s size with Styles’ athleticism, and I would take Styles in that scenario. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE NFL.com Colts vs. Commanders: Three must-know storylines for NFL Week 4 London game Can receivers take advantage of struggling DBs? In a matchup featuring two down defenses, it’s paramount for each offense to identify areas of vulnerability to attack. Those soft spots lie in the secondaries of both Ds, meaning the offenses will aim to exploit advantages with their receivers. The Colts will be looking to new WR1 Josh Downs, who took up the mantle left by the injured Alec Pierce and departed Michael Pittman. Downs has averaged a team-high 2.4 yards per route on a 32.8% target rate in Weeks 2 and 3 — while the Colts have mostly been without Pierce — and ranks 15th among qualified receivers in receiving expected points added (+12.6), just below Justin Jefferson, per Next Gen Stats. Indy will hope to get him in positions against Mike Sainristil, who has allowed a league-high five touchdowns and a 142.4 passer rating when targeted through three weeks. His defensive back mates, Jeremy Reaves (154.6 rating, +42.8% CROE) and Quan Martin (+28% CROE), have fared no better, opening up opportunities for Keenan Allen (barring a groin issue keeping him out) and tight end Tyler Warren. Meanwhile, Washington will look to exploit Justin Walley in the slot. The Colts primary nickelback has allowed 13 receptions on 15 targets for 213 yards and two TDs in the slot, the most yards allowed by any defender and 84 more than the next-closest CB. Opponents have recorded a perfect 158.3 passer rating when targeting Walley in those matchups, per Next Gen Stats. That could spell a big day for the Commanders’ top three receivers: two-time Pro Bowler Terry McLaurin, who’s looking for his first 100-yard game in 2026 but is questionable with a balky hamstring; rookie Antonio Williams, who boasts a team-high +27.2% CROE and +8.7 receiving EPA when targeted in the slot; and veteran Stefon Diggs, who has run a team-high 44 routes out of the slot this season. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com 3 keys to Commanders vs. Colts Win on third down The Commanders only converted three third downs against the Seahawks, although their final two of the day were some of the most important of the game. They moved the markers on a third-and-9 and third-and-7 thanks to runs from Rachaad White and Marcus Mariota, respectively, that sealed the victory. They had one prior to that drive, and many of those struggles can be credited to their own mistakes as much as the Seahawks’ defensive talent. Washington was plagued by multiple pre-snap penalties against the Seahawks. The most damning was an illegal formation that wiped away a 48-yard touchdown from Jacory Croskey-Merritt, but there were others that made manageable downs even more difficult. A false start from Josh Conerly moved them back five yards after an 11-yard gain. Another from John Bates turned a second-and-7 into a second-and-12. In the third quarter, an illegal shift turned a second-and-13 into a second-and-18. The Commanders punted two plays after that. While the Commanders obviously need to execute on third down against a Colts defense that ranks 10th in getting their opponents off the field, they also need to make third downs easier on themselves. It will allow them to get in a rhythm, and as they showed last week, they can compete against the best defenses in the league when that happens. Follow the action and share every cheer, question and instant reaction with fellow fans on the SB Nation app. Chat live during every game Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly move between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Sports Illustrated Washington’s Linebacker Room Changed While Frankie Luvu Was Gone While Luvu was out, Sonny Styles’ role changed quickly . He went from playing 48 of 55 defensive snaps in Philadelphia to handling the green dot and playing all 67 against Seattle. The rookie finished that game with five tackles, two passes defended, an interception and a forced fumble, but the bigger development may have been everything the Commanders were asking him to handle before the snap . Then came another change nobody wanted, or saw coming. Leo Chenal suffered a neck fracture against Seattle that required surgery and ended his season. Suddenly, Kain Medrano was needed for 44 defensive snaps after entering the game without a defensive snap on his NFL resume. He responded by taking an interception 50 yards for a touchdown in the fourth quarter. So while Washington lost another piece of the linebacker room, it also found out Medrano could handle being thrown directly into the fire. Now Luvu returns, and Jones doesn’t sound like someone interested in taking anything away from Styles because of it. When asked Thursday how Luvu’s return could affect the rookie’s growing responsibilities, Jones said the plan hasn’t really changed. title: Who gets credit for Commanders upset of Seahawks? – survey results
summary: Sunday’s 33-31 upset over the Seattle Seahawks did a lot more than just put a mark in the win column. It gave Commanders fans a collective sigh of relief and brought back an energy that seemed completely sapped just seven days earlier. In this week’s Reacts survey, we dug into two key areas: our regular […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 27: Players of the Washington Commanders pose for a photo during the second half against the Seattle Seahawks at Northwest Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sunday’s 33-31 upset over the Seattle Seahawks did a lot more than just put a mark in the win column. It gave Commanders fans a collective sigh of relief and brought back an energy that seemed completely sapped just seven days earlier. In this week’s Reacts survey , we dug into two key areas: our regular check-in on fan confidence, and an evaluation of which unit deserved the lion’s share of the credit for pulling off the home upset. Here is how the votes shook out and what our community had to say. Question 1: Are you confident in the team’s direction? The rollercoaster ride continues. After opening at 70% in Week 1 and ticking up to 80% following Week 2, the bottom fell out in Week 3 at a dismal 20%. One week and one signature upset later, that number has bounced right back up to 76%. Whether this jump represents genuine long-term faith or simply immediate postgame relief following the win in the home opener vs the Seashawks, the mood around the fanbase has clearly turned back toward the positive. Still, a few regular commenters were quick to separate game-day emotion from long-term trajectory. Others are keeping their guard up. By the way, here are this week’s results of the confidence question from the other NFC East teams: Question 2: Which phase of the game was most instrumental in the Commanders win over the Seahawks on Sunday? Visit our partners at FanDuel Nearly half the votes went to the offense with just over a third to defense, but reading through the comments, our community wasn’t ready to let David Blough take a solo victory lap. Defense: The reality is that Sunday was a clinic in complementary football. Daronte Jones’ defense repeatedly bailed out the team by clamping down on Seattle’s ground attack and generating 3 critical takeaways—none bigger than the second-half pick-six that completely flipped momentum. Game-winning INT 40 snaps into his career 🤯 Kain Medrano’s already making game-changing plays for the @Commanders . pic.twitter.com/T7cNOSDBHd — NFL Films (@NFLFilms) September 30, 2026 Offense: At the same time, when Blough’s offense had to have a drive in the fourth quarter, Marcus Mariota settled down, shook off that rough 1-for-11 third-down mark, and led a clutch scoring march that drained the clock and sealed the win. Rachaad White with the big run to keep the drive going! @SEAvsWAS on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/8miKbMKu7c — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 Special Teams: Then there is the third phase that often gets forgotten: special teams. In a game decided by just 2 points, rookie kicker Drew Stevens was dead-eye reliable on 3-pointers. He nailed both of his field goal tries under immense pressure (we won’t talk about the missed 48-yard PAT following the penalty on Frankie Luvu, who wasn’t even playing in the game). Without Stevens doing his field-goal kicking job cleanly, all the defensive takeaways in the world might not have been enough. DQ: The 19% of respondents who gave their vote to Dan Quinn probably may have been onto something: nobody carried this team across the finish line alone. When a team plays together and comes away with a win in difficult circumstances, the head coach has to get some credit for that, right? Wrapping up the thought When a squad is banged up and leaning on backups in critical spots, winning doesn’t come down to a single playcaller having a stroke of genius. It requires all three phases covering for one another when things go sideways. Daronte Jones’ defense provided the short fields and the splash plays, David Blough’s offense capitalized with a clutch, clock-killing touchdown drive when it mattered most, and Drew Stevens quietly put 6 points on the board to make sure no offensive drives that crossed midfield prior to the 2-minute warning were wasted. That is textbook complementary football, and fostering that kind of buy-in across the roster is ultimately the head coach’s job. Next up: a Week 4 international showdown in London against Daniel Jones and the Indianapolis Colts Holding onto the team’s collective resilience will be vital as Washington packs its bags for London. With a quick turnaround, international travel logistics, and an Indianapolis team eager to turn Daniel Jones loose against his old NFC East rival, the Commanders won’t have the luxury of relying on just one side of the ball. If Sunday proved anything, it’s that this team’s margin for error is razor-thin—and their best chance to keep stacking wins is by doing it together. Per Fan Duel, Indianapolis is currently favored on Sunday. title: NFL Week 4 uniforms: Browns wearing 'Alpha Dawg' look; Giants go 'Legacy'
summary: Here's a look at what each NFL team is wearing in Week 4, led by an alternate look from the Cleveland Browns.
full_text:
As the calendar turns to October, NFL uniforms remain as fresh as ever with an alternate-heavy slate in Week 4. 

 

 On "Thursday Night Football," the Cleveland Browns will wear their  "Alpha Dawg"  combination against the Pittsburgh Steelers . Cleveland revealed the all-brown threads in July 2025 with a brand new alternate brown helmet. They debuted last season and marked the first time in franchise history that a brown helmet was worn. Orange-colored numbers run across the front and back of the jersey, as well as on the shoulder. There's also an orange stripe on the helmet.

 In the throwback space, the New York Giants are donning their legacy uniforms against the Arizona Cardinals . New York wore these threads from 1980 to 1999. It was reintroduced in 2022, when the team brought back the navy helmet. Other design elements include classic numbers plus the red-and-blue trim on the jerseys and pants, similar to the uniforms of the 1980s and '90s. Written inside the collar is "Once a Giants, Always a Giant," the words of late owner Wellington Mara. 

 The Carolina Panthers , meanwhile, will bring an all-black look to "Sunday Night Football" against the Detroit Lions . Carolina first debuted this all-black combination in 2022. 

 The Dallas Cowboys are rocking navy blue alternates with silver pants against the Houston Texans , a look the team will wear only a handful of times each season. The Texans will wear liberty white jerseys with deep steel blue pants. It marks the same uniform matchup the Texans and Cowboys wore for Houston's first regular-season game as a franchise in 2002. 

 The New Orleans Saints and Atlanta Falcons on Monday will honor the 20th anniversary of the Saints' return to the Superdome following Hurricane Katrina by wearing the same uniform combinations they wore for the emotional and memorable "Monday Night Football" matchup on Sept. 25, 2006. The Saints will wear white jerseys and gold pants, and the Falcons will be in their red jerseys and white pants.

title: Why Bill Parcells considers Jacoby Brissett to be like a son
summary: Bill Parcells has been a mentor to Jacoby Brissett since high school, guiding him through football and life decisions.
full_text:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- Twice a year since high school, Jacoby Brissett walked into Duffy's Sports Grill in Jupiter, Florida, and headed to the round booth in the corner for a lunchtime "Board of Directors" meeting.

 Except Brissett wasn't on the board of any organization, charity or company. And this certainly wasn't a conference room. His meetings were just three guys around a table talking about life and football -- which, for them, is largely one and the same.

 If there's a chairman of this mythical board, it's Pro Football Hall of Fame coach Bill Parcells, who named this biannual lunch that includes Brissett and his longtime friend and adviser Abe Elam.

 "We just sit and start talking," Brissett told ESPN.

 The conversation can range from Brissett starting at quarterback for the Arizona Cardinals  to Parcells' old team, the New York Giants , with whom he won two Super Bowls. The teams converge Sunday when the Giants host the Cardinals (1 p.m. ET, CBS).

 Parcells, who turned 85 in late August, spends his summers in upstate New York and winters on the east coast of Florida. He and Brissett will talk after Sunday's game just as they have after each of the first three games of the season. They meet when both are in Florida, even if it's not at Duffy's, which has closed.

 They'll talk football, but the relationship transcends sports. Parcells is one of the most important figures in the life of Brissett, 33. Their friendship spans nearly 20 years, back to when Parcells befriended Brissett's high school coach and started hanging around practices at William T. Dwyer High School in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. He became a mentor to Brissett, guiding him in finances, professionalism and, of course, football.

 In return, Parcells gained a willing pupil who parlayed his guidance into an 11-year NFL career. Brissett may not be the most talented QB Parcells has coached but lasting that long in the league is a testament to the intangibles that drew Parcells into the relationship.

 "I had three daughters; he's like a son," Parcells told ESPN. "That really is what the relationship is, in the respect that I look at it. And my job is just to try to guide and be direct as I can without being a nuisance and without badgering him and without doing anything or telling him, 'This is what you need to do. This is how you need to try to go forward in this business.'

 "And he's a very good listener, and he's done everything right in his career in terms of trying to prepare, getting ready physically, getting ready mentally. And he's been very good with his finances. He's a very good listener about that. And I'm just proud of him. I love him."

 

 Why Brissett believes he wouldn't be in the NFL if not for Parcells 

 Football wasn't Brissett's priority in high school. Far from it. In his mind, he was destined to play basketball. So, when Brissett met Parcells early in his high school career, Brissett didn't really know this older man coming to watch him practice.

 "The funny thing is, I hated football," Brissett said.

 "Then, as my high school coach started to explain the magnitude of who this guy was, obviously I watched football, but I never got super invested, and then over time, we spent so much time together, all the stories he tells me like, 'Hey, be expecting this and be prepared for this along your journey,' and stuff like that, and I'm like, the amount of times since he's been right to the point where I'm like, 'God dang, I got to start listening to this man.' His track record is pretty good."

 In Brissett, Parcells saw a kindred spirit, albeit one 50 years younger.

 "We both liked football and I could see he was a committed player," Parcells said. "He was anxious to learn and we talked not only about football, but a lot of different things in life."

 During lunch after the second time they met, Parcells told a teenage Brissett how they were similar.

 "He goes, 'You know, you're just like me. I'm white. You're Black. But we're the same person,'" Brissett recalled. "I'm like, 'How the hell are we the same? You're 65 and I'm 14.'"

 Once they began talking about themselves, their families, how much they love football, Brissett saw it.

 "I'm like, 'I got a lot in common with this old man.'"

 

 From then on, Parcells was there for Brissett.

 Whatever decision Brissett made throughout his career, Parcells supported. He encouraged Brissett to stick with football after high school, even though Brissett split snaps in high school with a quarterback who didn't play beyond their senior year. When Brissett decided to play quarterback at the University of Florida, Jeff Driskel , who was the top-rated prep quarterback the same year, was waiting for him in Gainesville. That didn't matter to Parcells. He didn't just tell Brissett it was the right decision. He reaffirmed it to him.

 "Here's what he's got going for him: First of all, he's very committed to the game. He loves the game. He loves playing. He's committed mentally, physically, and he just wants to be good at what he does," Parcells said. "And once you see that trait and you're a coach, you want to do everything you can to assist him."

 Even get down in the mud.

 One day while Brissett was preparing for the 2016 NFL combine, he was throwing routes on the field at his old high school in the rain, and Parcells, then 75, was on his knees in the mud snapping to Brissett.

 That memory still pops into Brissett's mind whenever Parcells texts the same thing after something good happens to Brissett: "I'm so proud of you. This is what we worked for."

 "I always tell him, 'Man, I would not be here if it wasn't for you,'" Brissett said. "I legit would probably be working at T-Mobile, no disrespect to T-Mobile, but something else.

 "Even to this day, he's still like, 'Send me videos of your workout. Let me see you in the gym in the offseason.' In the offseason, he goes, 'I want to make sure you're doing what you're supposed to be doing.' And he is legit. I sent him a video, he's telling me about my form. I'm like, 'You're a football coach, not a weightlifting coach.' But stuff like that. And it's like we've gotten to that point."

 Why Parcells persuaded Brissett to skip a rookie event 

 Not a conversation goes by, whether it's in person or on the phone, that Parcells doesn't remind Brissett to save his money. It doesn't happen once per conversation, but twice. It's typically the first thing Parcells brings up -- "You saving your money?" -- and the last thing he says before hanging up -- "Hey, make sure you keep saving your money."

 Brissett's money was an offseason storyline as he refused to participate in voluntary offseason OTAs and minicamp because of a contract dispute, and he held in -- attended but didn't participate -- during the mandatory minicamp in June. He reached agreement on July 26 on a $15.5 million guaranteed contract with a chance to make $21 million with incentives.

 Parcells has been a voice of reason and direction for Brissett, using a no-nonsense approach with nonstop support to get his message across. Parcells has spent years telling Brissett what he didn't want to hear but rather what he needed to hear, Elam said.

 It has helped Brissett become more self-aware and build self-confidence because he quickly realized that Parcells has been around long enough to know what's coming before it happens.

 During Brissett's rookie year with the Patriots, he was invited to the annual NFLPA rookie premiere in Los Angeles along with some teammates. The multiday event includes business seminars, networking and photo shoots. Parcells called Brissett and told him not to go. Brissett paused. He wanted to go. Parcells thought Brissett had a chance to play early that season while Tom Brady was suspended for four games because of his role in Deflategate.

 "It'll mean a lot if you stayed," Parcells told Brissett.

 

 Brissett listened. He stayed in Massachusetts, but it wasn't like he got extra time with…

title: All-time rosters for 23 teams with multiple Super Bowls
summary: This was no small task, but 13 players ended up making more than one all-time SB roster.
full_text:
ESPN will televise the Super Bowl for the first time in February 2027. We will count down to the big game with Super Bowl-centric stories every month. 

 Picking an all-time Super Bowl team for Super Bowls I-XL would be a difficult task, matching up players from different eras, under different rules and different schematics, but a lot of the names would be familiar and mostly Hall of Fame worthy.

 Picking an all-time Super Bowl team for each individual franchise is a little trickier.

 Twenty-three teams have played in multiple Super Bowls. Our goal was to come up with an all-time roster for each of those franchises, leaning toward the success those players had in the Super Bowls in which they played, regardless of the success of their overall career or in that particular season(s).

 As an example, Larry Brown was one of the Dallas Cowboys ' choices at cornerback, not Hall of Famer Deion Sanders .

 Why? Brown intercepted two passes in Super Bowl XXX and was named the game's Most Valuable Player.

 Across all of the 23 rosters, 13 players were selected for two franchises' all-time Super Bowl teams, including four former New England Patriots : QB  Tom Brady (Buccaneers), K  Adam Vinatieri (Colts), G  Joe Thuney (Chiefs) and TE  Rob Gronkowski (Buccaneers).

 Here are the selections made by our NFL Nation reporters:

 The Super Bowl LI team accounts for most of the selections given how potent the Falcons were on offense in that game despite the historic blowing of that 28-3 lead. Matt Ryan was 17-of-23 passing for 284 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions, outplaying his New England Patriots counterpart, Tom Brady. Julio Jones had 87 yards on four catches, Devonta Freeman ran for 75 yards and a touchdown, and Austin Hooper added a touchdown.

 Terance Mathis made a case for WR1 with seven catches for 85 yards and a touchdown in Super Bowl XXXIII, but it's hard to pick against Jones. The Super Bowl LI team led the way on defense, too. Grady Jarrett had three sacks, Robert Alford had a pick-six and Deion Jones was a standout. The Falcons had no sacks of John Elway in Super Bowl XXXIII, but Ronnie Bradford did intercept him. The easiest pick overall might have been Tim Dwight, who had 210 yards in kick returns in Super Bowl XXXIII, including a 94-yard touchdown. -- Marc Raimondi

 When it comes to the Ravens' two Super Bowl championship teams, it was nearly a clear-cut split considering the 2000 team was carried by Ray Lewis and defense and the 2012 one was led by Joe Flacco and the offense.

 The offensive players from the 2000 team who made the all-time Super Bowl team were left tackle Jonathan Ogden, who is in the Pro Football Hall of Fame; running back Jamal Lewis, who ran for 102 yards and a touchdown in the Super Bowl; tight end Shannon Sharpe, who delivered big plays throughout the postseason; and wide receiver Brandon Stokley, who scored the franchise's first touchdown in a Super Bowl.

 The defensive players from the 2012 team were middle linebacker Lewis, who was also the Super Bowl MVP in 2000; cornerback Jimmy Smith, who broke up a fourth-down pass in the final two minutes; and safety Ed Reed, who intercepted 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick in the second quarter. -- Jamison Hensley
