title: What are the top 10 upsets in Super Bowl history?
summary: What are the biggest upsets in Super Bowl history? The Patriots, Jets, Giants, Eagles, Seahawks and others make their cases.
full_text:
The Super Bowl represents a matchup between the two best teams in the NFL that season, but some matchups are more lopsided than others.

 On paper, at least.

 We've seen undefeated juggernauts, record-setting offenses and burgeoning dynasties take the field on the NFL's biggest stage with the public expecting those teams to hoist the Lombardi Trophy, only to fall to backup quarterbacks, double-digit underdogs and habitual Super Bowl losers.

 

 Of the 60 Super Bowls that have taken place since 1967, we examined the 10 biggest upsets using a variety of data points: pregame spread, margin of victory and cultural impact. Some teams are repeat underdogs (we're looking at you, New York Giants ), while others were so dominant in their era that any loss they suffered in a Super Bowl was considered an upset.

 Here are the 10 biggest upsets in Super Bowl history, starting with the game that had the 1972 Dolphins popping champagne yet again.

 COUNTDOWN TO SUPER BOWL LXI: ESPN will televise the Super Bowl for the first time in February. We are counting down to the big game with a Super Bowl Top 10 series, featuring rankings on everything from best catches and performances to biggest upsets, that will run every other Sunday leading up to Super Bowl LXI on Feb. 14, 2027. 

 
 

 1. Giants over Patriots, SB XLII 
 When: Feb. 3, 2008

 Where: University of Phoenix Stadium (Glendale, Ariz.)

 Pregame betting line:  Patriots -12

 Final Score: Giants 17, Patriots 14

 The 2007 New England Patriots were the closest team to matching the 1972 Miami Dolphins ' undefeated season -- the only one in NFL history. But by season's end, the Dolphins' cherished record remained intact.

 The Patriots completed a 16-0 regular season thanks to the league's No. 1 offense and record-setting seasons from wide receiver Randy Moss and quarterback Tom Brady, who won his first regular-season MVP. After consecutive multiple-score wins against the Jaguars and Chargers to kick off their playoff run, the Patriots needed only a win in Super Bowl XLII over a New York Giants team that owned the lowest point differential of any playoff team that season. The teams previously faced off in the regular-season finale, during which the Giants had held the largest lead over New England of any team on its schedule; New England came back from a 12-point deficit to win.

 The game at University of Phoenix (now State Farm) Stadium was a defensive battle and remained a one-score game until early in the fourth quarter. New England took a four-point lead late in the quarter, but Giants quarterback Eli Manning led a 12-play, 83-yard touchdown drive that featured one of the greatest plays in Super Bowl history.

 On third-and-5, Manning evaded pressure and launched a jump ball 32 yards downfield to unheralded wide receiver David Tyree, who pinned the ball against his helmet to complete the catch. Manning also converted a third-and-11 with a 12-yard completion to Steve Smith before finding Plaxico Burress for a 13-yard, game-winning touchdown.

 No team since has come so close to a perfect season. The Patriots would get an opportunity for revenge four years later, but we'll address that game soon...

 
 

 2. Patriots over Rams, SB XXXVI 
 When: Feb. 3, 2002

 Where: Louisiana Superdome (New Orleans)

 Pregame betting line:  Rams -14

 Final Score: Patriots 20, Rams 17

 This was the game that birthed a dynasty.

 On one side were the St. Louis Rams, aka "the Greatest Show on Turf." Mike Martz's squad, which had won the Super Bowl two years earlier, featured a pair of 1,000-yard receivers in Isaac Bruce and Tory Holt, and the NFL's Offensive Player of the Year in running back Marshall Faulk. The Rams' defense also improved from 31st in scoring in 2000 to seventh in 2001.

 Meanwhile, the Patriots, in their second season under coach Bill Belichick, were led by Brady, a relatively unknown second-year quarterback who had taken over the starting job in Week 3 after an injury to Drew Bledsoe.

 New England held a 17-3 lead going into the fourth quarter, but Rams quarterback Kurt Warner ran for a touchdown and then threw another to tie the score with 90 seconds remaining. Brady then led the Patriots on a nine-play, 53-yard drive to set up Adam Vinatieri's game-winning 48-yard field goal.

 The Patriots went on to win six Super Bowls during Brady's 20-season tenure in New England, establishing arguably the greatest NFL dynasty -- and it started with that upset win in New Orleans.

 
 

 3. Jets over Colts, SB III 
 When: Jan. 12, 1969

 Where: Orange Bowl (Miami)

 Pregame betting line:  Colts -18

 Final Score: Jets 16, Colts 7

 The third AFL-NFL championship game was technically the first "Super Bowl" and featured Baltimore Colts coach Don Shula, who would eventually set the record as the winningest coach in NFL history.

 But he did not win this game.

 The AFL and NFL were still separate leagues, although a merger was in motion. The NFL won the previous two championship games against the AFL and was widely believed to be the better league. Those beliefs didn't stop quarterback Joe Namath of the AFL Jets from calling his shot similar to Babe Ruth.

 "We're going to win," he said to the Miami Touchdown Club crowd during Super Bowl week. "I guarantee it."

 Broadway Joe backed up his claim, outdueling "Golden Arm" Colts quarterback Johnny Unitas and leading New York to a 16-0 lead before the Colts scored a touchdown in vain late in the fourth quarter. This remains the biggest upset in Super Bowl history in terms of pregame spread, and is also the only Super Bowl matchup that currently can't be repeated. The leagues officially merged in 1970, and both teams have played in the same conference ever since.

 

 

 4. Eagles over Patriots, SB LII 
 When: Feb. 4, 2018

 Where: U.S. Bank Stadium (Minneapolis)

 Pregame betting line:  Patriots -4.5

 Final Score: Eagles 41, Patriots 33

 By the 2017 season, the Patriots' dynasty had endured a lull (by its standards), but was entering possibly its most dominant era and was on the brink of winning its third Super Bowl in four seasons.

 Brady won his third regular-season MVP award, and New England owned the league's top-ranked offense and fifth-best scoring defense. The Patriots hadn't lost in nearly two months by the time they got to U.S. Bank Stadium in February, but the Eagles were a top-five scoring offense and defense, thanks in large part to MVP-caliber play from quarterback Carson Wentz .

 But Wentz tore his ACL in Week 14, and backup Nick Foles started the remaining nine games of the season, including the playoffs.

 Foles cemented himself in Philadelphia lore with the "Philly Special" -- an end-around reverse pass in which he caught a touchdown at the end of the first half to give the Eagles a two-score lead. Naturally, the Patriots rallied to take a one-point lead in the fourth quarter, but Foles sealed a victory with a touchdown pass to Zach Ertz with just over two minutes remaining in the game.

 This marked the Eagles' first Super Bowl victory and served as revenge for their loss to New England in Super Bowl XXXIX.

 

 

 5. Broncos over Packers, SB XXXII 
 When: Jan. 25, 1998

 Where: Qualcomm Stadium (San Diego)

 Pregame betting line:  Packers -11

 Final Score: Broncos 31, Packers 24

 The fourth time was the charm for Broncos quarterback John Elway, who had lost his three previous Super Bowl appearances before finally breaking through.

 The reigning champion Packers were led by their own future Hall of Famer, Brett Favre, who won his third consecutive MVP award in 1997. They owned the NFL's second-ranked scoring offense but also a top-five defense. Denver had lost three Super Bowls in four seasons from 1986 to 1989, but underwent a resurgence under coach Mike Shanahan, particularly Elway, who was 37 and nearing the end of his career in 1997.

 Green Bay jumped out to a 7-0 lead before the Broncos scored 17 unanswered points. Both teams traded scores…

title: NFL Week 4 betting guide: Analysis and top plays for Sunday's games
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 4 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: find betting value.

 Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league.

 From spreads and moneylines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. With that, let's dive into our best bets, favorite defensive props and the top game to bet in Week 4.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Jump to: 
 Bowen's Game of the Week  | Solak's plays  | Walder's props 

 

 

 Bowen's Game of the Week 

 New England Patriots at Buffalo Bills (-6.5, 48.5) 
1 p.m. ET on CBS, Highmark Stadium, Orchard Park, New York

 

 The Buffalo Bills , the AFC favorite to reach the Super Bowl, will host last season's AFC Super Bowl representative, the New England Patriots , in a matchup of AFC East rivals Sunday.

 The Patriots will need game plan answers on both sides of the ball to counter the Bills' high-scoring offense, and they'll have to create a more defined passing game without A.J. Brown  (ankle) on the field. I like the Bills to win and cover in this one, and in a divisional game with this level of coaching and familiarity, I'll take the under on the total. Let's check out both clubs, and I'll add some props at the end to play, too.

 

 When the Bills have the ball: In their Week 3 win over the Chargers, the Bills failed to control offensive tempo, and they turned the ball over. It happens in this league. But don't let one game change the narrative on an explosive Bills offense leading the NFL in scoring (33.7 PPG) and producing top-10 numbers in both passing and rushing. Quarterback Josh Allen will see heavy single-high coverage from New England (both man and zone), which creates opportunities for the Bills to scheme for crossing concepts and big-play throws on deep over routes, and they can also attack the seams with tight end Dalton Kincaid . The man matchup to watch to here is DJ Moore against Christian Gonzalez (shoulder), if the Patriots corner is up for the game. Best versus best.

 And let's not forget the offensive balance the Bills have with running back  James Cook III , who has produced back-to-back games with at least 135 yards rushing, against a New England defense allowing 4.8 YPC. The question I always have for teams versus Allen, given his dual-threat ability, is how much man coverage can you play? And what is your answer for Allen as a runner in the low red zone? Let's see how the Patriots counter, as Allen has rushed for two scores in all three games played this season. He's the league's ultimate difference-maker.

 When the Patriots have the ball: Quarterback Drake Maye has made some reckless decisions with the ball, throwing a league-high six interceptions and registering a 45.9 QBR (25th in the league). But I'm not going to put this all on Maye, as the Patriots' wide receiver group is lacking juice and matchup edges. With Brown on IR, who is the boundary X to win the one-on-ones? The tape shows us that the New England wideouts aren't creating separation at a high rate. The key here is for Patriots offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels to scheme more defined throws -- while having answers to pressure -- versus a Bills defense that has been more zone-heavy (65.9% of opponent dropbacks). Maye is going to see split-safety coverage. Lift the safeties here and create those middle-of-the-field voids for the quarterback to drive the ball.

 More importantly, the Patriots need to generate some run-game efficiency with Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson to get the Bills out of two-deep coverage. The Patriots are averaging 3.9 YPC  (20th in the league) with an explosive run rate of 8.2% (25th). No question on the numbers here. They are down. Let's see how McDaniels game-plans for Jim Leonhard and the Bills' new defensive scheme to get his QB rolling again. And it wouldn't surprise me if the Patriots try to muddy this one up with a ball control/play-action script.

 Now, let's get to some prop bets ...

 

 James Cook III rushing yards OVER 88.5 (-111) 

 As mentioned, Cook has rushed for 135-plus in two straight, and he's averaging 19.3 carries per game. Plus, Cook has 12 rushes of 10 or more yards this season. Take the steady volume and the explosive-play ability here.

 Hunter Henry receiving yards OVER 30.5 (-110) 

 Henry has topped the 31-yard mark just once this season, and he was held to just one reception in the Week 3 loss to Jacksonville. However, I see the tight end as an answer to the two-high zone coverage of the Bills. Henry can be the outlet for Maye, while also pressing the seams.

 DJ Moore receptions OVER 3.5 (-133) 

 The juice isn't friendly on this one, but that's a low reception total for Moore. In the two full games Moore has played (he left Week 2 early with an injury), he had at least five receptions in both. Look for the Bills to use motion to deploy Moore, getting him free access off the ball versus man coverage.

 

 

 
 Solak's plays 
 

 Detroit Lions -3.5 (-112) at Carolina Panthers 

 It's important to watch the forecast for this game as we get closer to kickoff. There's a good chance of rain showers Sunday night, and we know that Jared Goff 's performance as a passer can be impacted more by bad weather, given his smaller hands. But I still feel comfortable taking this bet at this number because of the Panthers' injury issues. Both starting cornerbacks are expected to miss this game, which all but precludes Carolina from playing man coverage against Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams . If the Panthers take a zone-heavy approach, expect Jahmyr Gibbs to run wild -- heck, expect Gibbs to run wild anyway, as the Panthers are giving up more rushing yards per game to running backs than any other defense. Have I mentioned the Panthers' passing defense is also among the league worst against tight ends?

 The Lions have Carolina outgunned offensively, and I'm not sure Bryce Young can keep scoring pace. Receiver Jalen Coker (quad) is questionable, three starting offensive linemen ( Ikem Ekwonu , Damien Lewis and Taylor Moton ) are out, and a key backup ( Monroe Freeling ) is in concussion protocol. Detroit's defense is extremely gettable through the air, but the Lions have enough pass rush power to generate sacks and turnovers such that the Panthers can't keep this shootout within one score.

 Los Angeles Rams -3 (-115) at Philadelphia Eagles 

 

 I would only take this line at -3 (up to -120) and not buy the hook, so move quickly here. DeVonta Smith missed practice Thursday with his hamstring injury, which officially moves him into the "seriously questionable" category as we approach Sunday. I already leaned to the Rams' side with a healthy Smith. If he can't go, the Eagles' receiver corps will feature Dontayvion Wicks , first-round rookie Makai Lemon and Hollywood Brown against the loaded Rams secondary. Remember, pass-catching tight end Dallas Goedert is also out with a knee injury.

 The Eagles' defense had a brutal night last Monday against the Chicago Bears ' passing attack, regularly suffering communication issues as the Bears sent receivers in motion. They get another motion-heavy passing attack in Sean McVay's Rams offense, which gets Puka Nacua back at a critical time -- at 1-2, the Rams need a road win to prevent the sirens from screaming in their Super Bowl-aspiring season. They also have a vengeance play here, as they gave up a big second-half lead to the Eagles last season ... then lost…

title: How to bet Lions-Panthers on 'SNF': Analysis, tips and top prop plays
summary: Odds, bets and analysis to help you bet Lions-Panthers on "Sunday Night Football."
full_text:
The Detroit Lions enter as the favorite on the road against the Carolina Panthers on "Sunday Night Football." The 2-1 Lions are coming off a 31-24 win over the New York Jets , while the Panthers fell to 1-2 after a 21-18 loss to the Cleveland Browns .

 

 Detroit has balance, with the ability to attack Carolina on the ground and through the air, forcing a depleted defense to choose where to commit help. Jahmyr Gibbs threatens the edges and makes defenders miss, while Amon-Ra St. Brown gives Jared Goff a reliable answer underneath. With cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson sidelined, Carolina has fewer options for covering Detroit's receivers without sacrificing support against the run.

 The Panthers do have a counter: they disguise their safety looks after the snap and defend play action well, potentially complicating Goff's reads when he turns his back to the defense. Carolina's offense faces a different problem. Bryce Young has shown he can beat man coverage, but protection breakdowns undermine those opportunities. Detroit's pressure can exploit an injured offensive line.

 If Young gets time, however, the Lions' vulnerable secondary offers openings for Tetairoa McMillan and Darren Waller , particularly with the Panthers likely leaning on quick throws to avoid sacks.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 
 I prefer Detroit -3.5 because Carolina's injuries make it difficult to see the Panthers consistently trading scores. Detroit has scored 31 points in every game, its offense still producing despite inconsistencies. Carolina could produce offensively and still fall short of covering if its depleted defense can't get enough stops.

 

 Over 50.5 is a tougher commitment. Even if Detroit reaches its average again, Carolina needs at least 20 to get us there. Waller offers a promising outlet at tight end against a Lions defense that has allowed six touchdowns to the position, but Young's protection (or lack of) makes sustained scoring less dependable.

 Sacks could kill possessions before that matchup advantage translates into points. The Panthers' aggressive passing approach keeps the over viable, especially if they spend the second half chasing the Lions. But that comeback production is something I'm less willing to count on.

 The spread and total don't have a clear edge on either side.

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 

 Jahmyr Gibbs 140+ rushing and receiving yards (-112) 

 Gibbs' workload travels across game scripts. Detroit can feed him carries while leading or find him through the air if Carolina stays close. The Panthers have allowed a league-worst 580 rushing yards on 5.7 yards per carry. That gives Gibbs room to produce on the ground, while his seven targets per game gives this wager another path beyond rushing production. We're backing a heavy workload against a defense struggling to stop the run.

 

 Darren Waller Anytime TD +260 

 Liz Loza: Waller has emerged as a legitimate part of the Panthers' offense. Not only has his snap share increased each week (34% to 43% to 49%), but his eight targets led the team last Sunday. He's also been active in the red area, recording two end zone looks and hauling in two touchdowns over three contests. He has a good shot at hitting pay dirt again in Week 4 versus the Lions, as six different tight ends have recorded a TD when facing Detroit.

title: Fantasy football last-minute pickups for Week 4: Raymond, Waller among top options
summary: If injuries or tough matchups have you seeking help, Matt Bowen provides options at each key position.
full_text:
At various points during the fantasy football season, injuries, bye weeks and breaking news can cause you to need reinforcements for your fantasy lineup. Every Friday throughout the 2026 NFL season, Matt Bowen will offer some late-week pickup options at each of the primary fantasy positions to help fill those holes, with an emphasis on deeper leagues. 

 Because of that, this column will focus mostly on players rostered in fewer than 50% of ESPN leagues, with occasional exceptions. 

 Looking at the Week 4 NFL slate -- and the available players -- I'll start with the wide receiver position. I have two veteran pass catchers who are seeing consistent volume and producing solid fantasy numbers. There are options at quarterback, too, and one signal-caller could be getting his top target back. We'll also hit on the running backs in line to see an increased role due to injury, plus I have a tight end and a defense to get into lineups.

 

 Wide receivers 

 Kalif Raymond , Chicago Bears (48.4% rostered; vs. Jets) 

 The Bears haven't announced whether Case Keenum or Tyson Bagent will start at QB for the Week 4 home game versus the Jets, but either way I'm still pushing for Raymond based on his route deployment in Ben Johnson's offense. Raymond scored 21 points in the Week 3 win over the Eagles, and he has at least five receptions in all three games played this season. Raymond will see the ball as an outlet on crossers, sit routes and unders, plus he has the speed to create big plays (deep over routes and verticals). Raymond fits as a WR3 this week.

 Dontayvion Wicks (44.7% rostered) and Makai Lemon , Philadelphia Eagles (47.6% rostered; vs. Rams) 

 

 DeVonta Smith (hamstring) has been downgraded to doubtful for Sunday's home game versus the Rams, so managers can pivot to Wicks or Lemon, as both should see a bump in target volume. Wicks scored 12 or more points in each of his first two games, with at least four targets in all three this season, while Lemon caught three of four targets for 29 yards in the Week 3 loss to the Bears. I'm really interested in seeing how Lemon performs with an expanded role. The rookie out of USC has the traits to win at the top of the route and he accelerates through the ball.

 Mack Hollins , New England Patriots (11.2% rostered; at Bills) 

 The Bills have been zone-heavy under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard, and they play from a two-deep safety look on 49.2% of opponent dropbacks. That works for Hollins, as he has the coverage awareness to find open voids on short-to-intermediate throws. Hollins caught six of nine targets for 87 yards in the Week 3 loss to the Jaguars (14.7 points), and he has seen at least five targets in two of three games played. He's a deeper-league option this week.

 Malik Washington , Miami Dolphins (23.3% rostered; at Vikings) 

 You can take a shot on Washington because of his versatility and expanding role. Washington caught five of a season-high 10 targets for 56 yards in the Week 3 loss to the Chiefs, plus he had two carries for five yards from backfield alignments. Washington has seen five or more targets in all three games this season, with at least one rushing attempt in the past two. The Vikings' pressure defense will create conflict for quarterback Malik Willis and Miami's protection schemes, but that unit is giving up the 10th-most points per game to opposing wide receivers.

 

 Quarterbacks 
 

 Marcus Mariota , Washington Commanders (18.4% rostered; at Colts) 

 

 I didn't see Mariota scoring 20.42 points on the Seahawks defense in Week 3. The veteran quarterback delivered the ball with timing and location, finishing with 183 yards and three touchdown passes. While I would like to see Mariota deployed more on designed carries, there is a clear connection here with Terry McLaurin (six receptions, 77 yards, one touchdown in Week 3), and we can't pass on this matchup versus Indianapolis. The Colts are allowing 276 yards passing per game (third most). Mariota is a solid QB2 in Week 4, while  Jayden Daniels (elbow) misses his second straight game.

 C.J. Stroud , Houston Texans (37.0% rostered; vs. Cowboys) 

 The touchdown numbers are down for Stroud (three), but he is scoring 15.4 fantasy PPG, plus he has added 54 yards rushing this season. And this Texans pass game could get a major boost if wide receiver Nico Collins (hamstring) is back Sunday. I really like the matchup versus a Dallas defense allowing 23.5 fantasy PPG to opposing QBs (third most). If Collins is a go, you can start Stroud as a QB2 in superflex formats.

 Sam Darnold , Seattle Seahawks (50.9% rostered; vs. Chargers) 

 Darnold dropped 27.66 points on the Commanders in Week 3, his first game back after suffering a glute injury early in the Week 1 opener versus the Patriots. Darnold turned the ball over twice in Washington, but he finished with 379 yards and four touchdown throws. With an elite No. 1 option in Jaxon Smith-Njigba (135 yards receiving per game), Darnold should be viewed as a quality QB2 this week versus a Chargers defense ranked 15th against opposing QBs.

 

 Running backs 
 

 Keaton Mitchell , Los Angeles Chargers (18.4% rostered; at Seahawks) 

 Mitchell had a season-high 11 touches in the Week 3 game versus Buffalo, finishing with 47 total yards and a touchdown, good for 13.7 points. We know he's an explosive change-of-pace runner behind Omarion Hampton (15 carries in Week 3), plus he can be schemed in the pass game. Mitchell has an ankle injury that we need to monitor, but if he's good to go this week, he has value as a flex in deeper leagues.

 Kendre Miller , New Orleans Saints (15.0% rostered; at Falcons) 

 

 Travis Etienne Jr . (hamstring, IR) is out for the forseeable future, so Miller should be back in the fold, sharing touches with Alvin Kamara in the Saints backfield. Miller saw six touches last week, and he had nine carries for 30 yards and a touchdown (on a low red zone attempt) in Week 1. I don't see a ton of upside here due to Kamara's usage in the game plan, plus the Falcons are allowing only 12.8 fantasy PPG to opposing running backs. But if you need to find an option in a deeper league, Miller will see the ball.

 Jaylen Wright , Miami Dolphins (23.3% rostered; vs. Vikings) 

 With De'Von Achane  (ACL) out for the season, Ollie Gordon II and Wright move into prominent roles in the Miami backfield. Gordon fits as the early-down runner with north/south traits, while Wright has the speed and traits to provide more perimeter/receiving upside. Wright has limited usage this season (three carries), but he did have two games of 12 or more points in 2025. It's a tough matchup against a Minnesota defense that ranks fourth versus running backs, so Wright should be a deeper-league option only.

 Isaiah Davis , New York Jets (7.4% rostered; at Bears) 

 Breece Hall (thigh) is out for this week, which moves Braelon Allen into the No. 1 role, while also opening the door for Davis to see work. Davis has yet to register a carry this season, but he averaged 5.5 YPC last season, posting three games with 10 or more points. He's a deeper-league flier who could produce some numbers against a Bears defense allowing 4.9 YPC.

 

 Tight end 
 

 Darren Waller , Carolina Panthers (26.3% rostered; vs. Lions) 

 Waller caught five of a season-high eight targets for 51 yards last week against the Browns, and he now has double-digit points in back-to-back games. With his increase in usage, plus the matchup versus a Lions defense that ranks dead last versus opposing tight ends, Waller should be in your lineup for Week 4.

 Chicago Bears (30.1% rostered; vs. Jets) 

 The Bears are getting pressure on the quarterback and playing opportunistic defense under coordinator Dennis Allen. This unit has at least two sacks in all three games played this season, and they've forced three turnovers in two of them. You can put Chicago is as your D/ST this week versus Jets quarterback Geno Smith , who has been…

title: Colts vs. Commanders, NFL London preview: ESPN experts on key players, matchups and predictions
summary: The NFL rolls into London this begin with a clash between the Indianapolis Colts and the Washington Commanders -- so we asked ESPN reporters Stephen Holder and John Keim for a preview.
full_text:
The NFL rolls into the United Kingdom this Sunday as the London Games begin with a clash between the Indianapolis Colts and the Washington Commanders at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Ahead of the game, ESPN asked Colts reporter Stephen Holder and Commanders reporter John Keim to assess their respective teams, the players UK fans should watch and where Sunday's matchup could be won and lost... 

 

 How would you sum up the season so far? 
 

 SH:  It's been a bit of a struggle. The Colts' early-season schedule was not favourable and that resulted in two consecutive losses to the Ravens and Chiefs to begin the season. Last Sunday's win against the Texans was much needed, but the Colts' offense is feeling the loss of star receiver Alec Pierce , who will be out of the lineup for at least several weeks with a heel injury. There are also questions about the Colts' defense, which was embarrassed in its first two games.

 -  NFL International Games: Schedule, UK times for matches in London, more 
 -  Colts vs. Commanders: NFL London kick-off time, how to watch in UK 

 

 JK: Injury filled. Again. Washington was devastated by injuries in 2025 and it was one reason the team stumbled to a 5-12 season. Already this year, they will have played two games with seven players projected as starters when camp opened. All but one  -- left tackle Laremy Tunsil -- are expected back soon. Considering that, they're fortunate to be 1-2 after opening at Philadelphia, at Dallas and then home vs. Seattle. The Commanders are without their top players at: quarterback, left tackle, cornerback, linebacker, safety and tight end. They're forced to use a linebacker who was fifth on the depth chart entering the season ( Kain Medrano ).

 What's the biggest thing we've learned about this team that we didn't know coming into the season? 
 

 SH:  It's taking longer than hoped for some of the new additions on defense to make an impact. The Colts changed five of their 11 starting players on defense this season, and that has proven to be a difficult transition. Whether it all works as designed is still an open question as we are just three games into the season.

 

 JK: Their run defense is excellent. Washington had hoped it would improve in this area, but that was the case each of the last two years as well but it never materialised. From 2024-25, the Commanders ranked 30th in rushing yards allowed and 26th in yards per carry. But the defensive line -- Javon Kinlaw , Tim Settle and Daron Payne -- has been excellent and the linebackers speed has been a big factor as well. Odafe Oweh earned a big contract because he can rush the passer, but he's been terrific at setting the edge.

 

 

 What's the mood around the team about travelling to London? 
 

 SH:  The Colts are treating this like most any other game. Spirits are good because they won their last game, their first win this season. But the Colts have been adamant about their policy of traveling late in the week for their European games, as they have done in each of their three trips to the continent. The Colts' plan was to fly Thursday night and arrive in London on Friday morning. They will then eat, relax and get acclimated before holding a short practice on Friday afternoon.

 

 JK: Upbeat. However, while they were pleased with the win over Seattle, the players and coach Dan Quinn emphasised that it was just one game and that they had areas to correct -- if they want to build on the win. So while the win over Seattle made the flight to London much better, they did not view it as "we've arrived" but want to use it as a steppingstone, as quarterback Marcus Mariota said. And that's why numerous players harped on what they could do better to make sure one win leads to another.

 

 Who's been the standout player so far -- and who should UK fans watch out for? 
 

 SH:  Running back Jonathan Taylor has picked up where he left off last season, when he was one of the top runners in the NFL. But he will draw more attention from defenses in the coming weeks because the absence of Pierce allows opponents to focus more on run defense. Washington has found success defending runners in the past two games, so it will be interesting to see which team wins in this particular subplot.

 

 JK: Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles . He's far from a finished product, but the seventh overall pick already has made an impact. With  Frankie Luvu  sidelined, he's responsible for relaying the plays into the huddle and he's adept at communicating before the snap as well. He already has an interception and a forced fumble as well as a sack. He accomplished something no other rookie has done for Washington: record an interception, a forced fumble and multiple passes defensed in the same game. His speed has made a big difference in coverage and his ability to chase ballcarriers. He'll have to develop coming downhill and taking on blockers, but for now he's playing fast enough -- and the line is helping enough -- to avoid them.

 

 What's the biggest concern around the team heading into this game? 
 

 SH:  The Colts were yielding a historic amount of yardage in their first two games, leaving them statistically as the worst defense in the NFL. The 417.3 yards per game the Colts are allowing, on average, from opponents is well below the NFL average of 329.5. While the Colts made noticeable strides in their win against Houston last Sunday, it remains to seen whether they can sustain that momentum.

 

 JK: Health. But we already covered that above. Their depth will continue to be tested until more starters return over the next couple weeks. That's obvious so let's take a look at something else: the pass coverage. Indianapolis does not have a dynamic passing attack -- quarterback Daniel Jones ranks 18th in number of pass attempts of 15 air yards or more and only has a 56.6 passer rating on such throws. But the Commanders' weakness has been coverage; they've allowed the sixth most passing yards and the second most passing touchdowns.

 Where do you think Sunday's game will be won and lost? 

 

 SH:  Neither defensive unit in this game has shown itself to be reliably good. Each is yielding more than 30 points per game. What this game likely will hinge on is the respective quarterbacks' ability to exploit the opposing defense. Jones has a slight edge in this area in my mind.

 

 JK: I'll say the ground game. The Colts have two outstanding corners in Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward to contend with Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs . But they rank 28th in yards per carry allowed. The Commanders have remained devoted to running -- with the fourth most attempts despite being only 16th in yards per carry. But they will stick with it, using both Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White . If Washington's defense has been excellent vs. the run, with 27 of 64 carries going for two yards or less -- but if the Commanders continue stopping the run they must have better lane discipline when rushing Jones.

 Who wins and why? 
 

 SH:  I'm picking the Colts by a slim margin. My rationale: If the Colts star cornerbacks Gardner and Ward can limit Washington's receivers -- the Colts believe them to be the strength of their team -- it will position the Colts to prevail. But that's a matchup Indianapolis has to win to get the victory.

 

 JK: I was afraid you'd ask this question. This is a toss-up game; two 1-2 teams who faced a tough early schedule. I'll go with Washington and the ability to control the ground game; the key will be whether they can limit explosive pass plays. Mariota showed a tonne of poise and calmness in the pocket last week. This is a massive game for Washington: Can it build off a terrific win? We'll bet that they will, but the confidence isn't high because of their health and the teams are fairly equal.

title: The history of Harbaugh, Herbert and a spiraling 0-3 Chargers team
summary: After a troubling start to the 2026 season, here's a realistic look at the current Chargers' state of affairs.﻿
full_text:
LOS ANGELES -- For almost all 67 years of their franchise history, the Los Angeles Chargers have been synonymous with disappointment coming in heartbreaking fashion .

 Coach Jim Harbaugh's arrival in January 2024 appeared to be a paradigm shift.

 Harbaugh was a month removed from coaching Michigan to a national championship. He was a top coaching candidate with a track record of winning. And Harbaugh chose the Chargers . A team that had just won five games in 2023 and desperately needed a change in culture.

 ​The excitement was palpable in Los Angeles. In a city of stars, the Chargers now had their own.

 

 ​At his introductory news conference, Harbaugh proclaimed the Chargers would win "multiple championships." Much of his confidence was rooted in star quarterback Justin Herbert , whom Harbaugh called a "crown jewel."

 ​Harbaugh was enthralled with Herbert's 6-foot-6, 235-pound frame, arm strength and running ability. The coach promised to build a team and staff around Herbert that would make them championship-caliber -- with the belief that Herbert was already good enough to get them there.

 ​"Protect him. Protect his environment. On the field, protect him," Harbaugh said at the time. "Also, beef up the run game and play-action pass and the dropback game. ... I think that we can be extraordinary there with the receivers we have and the quarterback."

 A week later, new general manager Joe Hortiz echoed Harbaugh: "We want to develop a really good run game. You build a great run game and a great offensive line, you protect your quarterback. I've seen it done year in and year out, where I came from. You help him by supporting him with players that help the entire offense."

 ​Yet two seasons later, Harbaugh and Hortiz haven't delivered on their promises. Instead, Herbert has been among the NFL's most pressured and hit quarterbacks, the Chargers' running game has remained average, and the team's pass catchers have disappointed.

 ​Herbert hasn't exactly held up his end of the bargain, either. Harbaugh did his part to lead this team from five wins to back-to-back 11-win playoff-berth seasons, relying on Herbert's elite play. But both playoff losses ended in embarrassing fashion for the Chargers, where Herbert uncharacteristically threw multiple interceptions and missed receivers, and his greatness vanished in the biggest of moments.

 ​The Harbaugh-Herbert partnership was supposed to bring this franchise championships. Instead, in their third season together, neither look like the best version of themselves. And this week, Harbaugh challenged his quarterback to " be better ."

 Harbaugh and Herbert will try to save a spiraling season, by turning around one of the NFL's worst offenses (fourth worst in the league in points per game 14.7), when the winless Chargers play the reigning Super Bowl-champion Seattle Seahawks on Sunday ( 4:25 p.m. ET, CBS ). ESPN's Football Power Index, which before the season gave the Chargers the fifth-best odds to make the Super Bowl, now gives the Bolts the third-worst odds at making the postseason.

 ​"Obviously not where we want to be," Herbert said. "And it starts with me."

 
 

 HABRAUGH TYPICALLY FLOATS around at Chargers practice. He's not a playcalling coach, leaving those responsibilities to his coordinators.

 ​On this day during a training camp practice ahead of Harbaugh's first season in 2024, he pulled fourth-string quarterback Casey Bauman out of the drill to correct his footwork on a handoff. Bauman was cut weeks later, but it didn't matter to the coach. The details were paramount for anyone in Chargers' powder blue.

 ​It's the only drill in which Harbaugh has been a regular participant in three seasons coaching this team, likely because dominant rushing offenses are where he's made a living in football.

 ​The San Francisco 49ers , whom he coached from 2011 to 2014, ranked second in yards per game (139.6) over that span. In his last season at Michigan, the Wolverines were third in the Big Ten in rushing yards per game (169.1).

 ​That's what made a Harbaugh-Herbert pairing so exciting. Herbert had never played with a dominant rusher. "Can you imagine Justin Herbert with a great running game?" former Chargers offensive coordinator Greg Roman said ahead of the 2024 season. "... We don't know, but I can imagine what it might look like."

 We still don't know.

 ​Since Harbaugh arrived, the Chargers' rushing offense has ranked 16th in yards per game (115.9), 19th in yards per rush (4.2) and 21st in runs of 10-plus yards. They've been slightly better this season, a backfield buoyed by 2025 first-round pick Omarion Hampton and Keaton Mitchell . The Chargers rank 14th in yards per rush (4.2) and 12th in rushing yards per game (113) and runs of 10-plus yards.

 

 But it still isn't the dominant ground game that has long been associated with Harbaugh teams.

 ​Their rushing issues mostly come down to personnel. Injuries have played a factor, but the Chargers haven't had any difference-makers on the interior offensive line. Hortiz's biggest signings have been guard Mekhi Becton -- who was released after one season -- and center Tyler Biadasz -- who suffered a season-ending left ACL injury in this year's training camp.

 Also, the poor line play has resulted in Herbert taking a beating and somewhat changing his play style. Since 2024, Herbert's 391 quarterback hits rank first, and the Chargers have allowed 112 sacks, which ranks fifth most in the league. According to ESPN Analytics/NFL Next Gen Stats, the Chargers' pass block win rate this season (45%) ranks 27th and is the team's second-lowest through three games since the metric was introduced in 2017.

 Because of the poor offensive line Herbert has been scrambling more than ever. Last season, he rushed for a career-high 498 rushing yards and the third most on the Chargers

 ​"He has taken too many [hits]," Harbaugh said last season. "It's very concerning. We've got to get better. We got to put him in a better position."

 ​A year later, Herbert is still among the league's most-hit quarterbacks, ranking fourth (34), but Harbaugh's tune has changed.

 
 

 ​ IT WAS THE fourth quarter of last season's Week 6 game against the Miami Dolphins , with just under 40 seconds remaining on second down. Herbert dropped back to pass and defensive end  Jaelan Phillips  had him dead to rights for a sack, but somehow Herbert shook him off. Herbert quickly found wide receiver Ladd McConkey for a 42-yard gain, and four plays later the Chargers nailed a game-winning field goal.

 ​The play was an example of why many see Herbert as one of the league's best, despite not having won a playoff game in six seasons. It's also why Harbaugh took the job -- to be paired with who he calls the most talented quarterback he has ever had.

 ​But too many times, this version of Herbert -- the one who pulls a miraculous play to put his team in position to win -- has vanished in the Chargers' biggest moments.

 ​The Chargers won 11 games in the past two seasons because of an elite defense and Herbert's ability to take over a game, but when asked to be the exact same player in the postseason, Herbert has failed.

 

 In his first season with Harbaugh, Herbert had a league-low three interceptions, but in their 32-12 wild-card loss to the Houston Texans , Herbert became the first player in NFL history to throw more interceptions in a playoff game (four) than in the regular season.

 He finished 14-of-32 passing (43.8%), the third-worst completion percentage in a playoff game in Chargers history and was sacked four times. After that game, Harbaugh defended Herbert, saying he played like a "complete beast."

 ​​The following January, Herbert shrunk again. This time in a 16-3 wild-card loss to the New England Patriots .

 ​Herbert had no interceptions in this game, but finished with just 159 passing yards. He missed wide-open receivers, drifted into six sacks, and again, looked like a different…

title: Evaluating the 3-0 Raiders' strong offensive start
summary: Yes, it has been a small sample size. But the head coach has made the Raiders' offense almost unrecognizable.
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- Klint Kubiak was one of the best playcallers in this offseason's hiring cycle, and how he has operated the  Las Vegas Raiders ' offense to start the season is one of the reasons the organization was willing to wait until he helped the Seattle Seahawks win Super Bowl LX before naming him the coach .

 The Raiders are in the midst of their first 3-0 start since 2021, the last time they made the postseason, and much of their success is due to Kubiak rejuvenating an offense that was one of the worst in the league in 2025.

 

 Under former coach Pete Carroll and offensive coordinator Chip Kelly, the Raiders averaged 14.2 points per game. That total has jumped to 29.3 points per game -- tied for seventh in the NFL.

 Las Vegas beginning the season with a functional offense despite an inconsistent rushing attack and its best playmaker, Brock Bowers , missing two games is a testament to Kubiak's playcalling, his ability to put players in the best positions to be successful and veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins ' command of the entire operation.

 The Raiders will face their biggest test, the Kansas City Chiefs , at home on Sunday ( 4:25 p.m. ET, CBS ) with a chance to take possession of first place in the AFC West.

 "[Kubiak is] aggressive," tight end Ian Thomas told ESPN. "[But] he knows when to pull back, and he'll take chances when he needs to. It's a combination of a little bit of everything."

 

 

 THREE GAMES IS  a small sample size. But differences from this season compared with last, when the Raiders won a total of three games, have been eye-popping.

 In 2025, Las Vegas ranked last in total yards per game (245.2), 30th in yards per play (4.4), 31st in offensive efficiency (20.72), 26th in red zone efficiency (50%), 28th in third-down conversion rate (33.8%) and 31st in EPA (minus-124.11).

 So far in 2026, Las Vegas is 17th in total yards per game (322.5), 13th in yards per play (5.2), 10th in offensive efficiency (55.58), 17th in red zone efficiency (55.6%), tied for 14th in third-down conversion rate (42.3%) and 14th in EPA (2.78).

 The Raiders also have the fifth-best points margin (10) after ranking 30th in that category in 2025.

 It shouldn't come as a surprise that Kubiak has come in and improved the offense. He did the same as the offensive coordinator for the Seahawks a year ago. Seattle averaged 28.4 points per game, which ranked second in franchise history.

 What's impressive is that Kubiak is having success with a Raiders offense that entered the season with no wide receivers with a 1,000-yard season. He has found multiple ways to win games and put points on the board while utilizing the talent at hand.

 The Raiders began the Kubiak era without Bowers, who underwent a meniscus trim procedure ahead of the season opener against the Miami Dolphins . Still, Bowers' two-week absence didn't hinder the offense like his injury absences did last season. Las Vegas defeated Miami and the  Los Angeles Chargers by double figures.

 

 Against the Dolphins, the Raiders were effective in the run game, with running back Ashton Jeanty rushing for 102 yards. In Week 2, Kubiak took advantage of the Chargers' defense through explosive plays, as Cousins had a pair of 40-plus-yard pass attempts, while  Tre Tucker  totaled 119 receiving yards. The victory in Los Angeles also saw Kubiak get players such as wideouts Cody White and Dareke Young  -- mostly known for special teams support -- involved in the passing game. White caught two touchdown passes, while Young made a crucial 27-yard catch in the second half.

 Tucker told ESPN that Kubiak's confidence when calling plays and believing in his players has contributed to their success. Cousins said Kubiak's greatest strength in running an offense is getting everyone on the same page.

 "I only say that not really off the sample size of the last three weeks, but more off of 2021 [with the Minnesota Vikings ], and even him being my quarterback coach in '19 and '20," Cousins said. "And I just appreciate that organizational skills, but also the desire to improve. I think at times we come back from a win, and he doesn't allow the outcome of a win to cause him to let his guard down on things that need to be coached hard, and that's comforting for me because I love kind of feeling like nothing's going to get past his watchful eye."

 

 ONE ELEMENT OF  the Raiders' offense that has been effective is their ability to disguise the run and pass game through heavy personnel groupings. That was on display during their 35-27 win over the New Orleans Saints in Week 3, which snapped a franchise-worst 39-game streak of regular-season games without scoring 30 points.

 During the team's opening drive, the Raiders were in 22 personnel (two tight ends, two running backs and one wide receiver) and positioned at New Orleans' 35-yard line. With Thomas, mostly known for his blocking ability, and fullback Connor Heyward on the field, it appeared Cousins would hand the ball off to Jeanty.

 Instead, Bowers -- who was lined up on the outside -- slipped behind safety Justin Reid and was left uncovered before securing Cousins' pass for an 18-yard reception. Las Vegas ended the drive with a field goal. In the second quarter, the Raiders were near the goal line, with Jeanty and Heyward in the backfield, when Cousins threw a play-action touchdown pass to tight end Michael Mayer .

 On 63 plays, the Raiders used 12 personnel (1 TE, 2 RB), 21 personnel (2 TE, 1 RB) and 22 personnel a combined 51 times (80.9%). As a whole, Las Vegas has used multiple running backs on 43.7% of its plays -- the second-highest rate behind the San Francisco 49ers -- and multiple tight ends at a rate of 50.5% -- fourth-highest.

 

 The Raiders have a chance to be even more effective when using heavy personnel groupings now that Bowers is back in the mix. Bowers was named AFC Offensive Player of the Week after he caught 10 passes for 116 yards and a touchdown in Week 3. During his performance, Bowers acted more like a wide receiver than a traditional tight end. He ran 10 routes out wide, 15 in the slot and only eight in tight alignment.

 "That's our name of the game. But more so, I think that's just his background," Tucker said. "Very multiple, and we can do a lot of things and put different players in different positions to make plays and have success."

 Cousins has been a good conductor, as well. His quick decision-making and knowledge of Kubiak's offense have allowed him to keep the offense rolling. He is tied for the most passing touchdowns in the league with nine. On top of that, he has a completion percentage of 67.4% and a passer rating of 107.2.

 Cousins is also the first QB in NFL history age 38 or older to begin a season with three touchdown passes in three straight games.

 "He has been a joy to play with," center Tyler Linderbaum said. "I mean, he's a competitor. ... He will do anything it takes to win. You want to play for a guy like that."

 

 Cousins' performance and the offensive line's improved pass protection have gone hand in hand. The unit has allowed only five sacks and posted a pass block win rate of 58.7% -- third-best in the league. Las Vegas ranked 22nd in pass-block win rate (60.7%) in 2025. Starting right tackle DJ Glaze has looked like a completely different player in Year 3. He has only allowed five pressures after giving up 15 pressures through the first three weeks of last season and 72 for the entire season.

 "[DJ is] somebody that's a smart football player," offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko said. "Shows up every day to work, but that's the mindset of that whole group."

 Handling the Chiefs' defense will be a tall task for Las Vegas. If the Raiders want to remain undefeated, they will need to establish a consistent run game. Rookie running back Mike Washington Jr . broke loose for a 35-yard touchdown run against New Orleans.

 But besides that, the team's rushing attack has been inconsistent over…

title: Patriots preach patience when it comes to receiver WR Romeo Doubs' modest start
summary: After the Patriots signed him to a four-year deal in March, Doubs is searching for his footing in the offense entering Week 4.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- Quick-hit thoughts and notes around the New England Patriots and NFL:

 1. Doubs' modest start: Receiver Romeo Doubs ' home in the Patriots' locker room reflects the high expectations that followed him from Green Bay to New England after he  signed a four-year, $68 million contract in March . Quarterback Drake Maye 's locker is on the end, with receiver A.J. Brown to his right. Then, veteran receiver Mack Hollins , Doubs and fourth-year pass catcher  DeMario 'Pop' Douglas  fill out the row of five lockers.

 The 1-2 Patriots are banking on Doubs' signing paying off, and Sunday would be the ideal time for a breakout as they try to keep up with quarterback Josh Allen and the 3-0 Bills in Orchard Park, New York ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 The early returns have been modest. Doubs, who spent his first four NFL seasons with the Packers, has totaled six receptions for 145 yards. He had a costly drop in a season-opening loss at Seattle and was penalized for offensive pass interference in last Sunday's blowout road loss to the Jaguars. His highlight was a three-catch, 96-yard performance in the Patriots' win over the Steelers in Week 2.

 Coaches and teammates remain convinced of what the soft-spoken Doubs can bring to the Patriots. They're also preaching patience, with coordinator Josh McDaniels noting, "There's always going to be a period of acclimation [when players join new teams]."

 

 For his part, Doubs, 26, isn't discouraged.

 "Anything in this league isn't easy to do. I wouldn't say that's just football; it's everywhere. You have to work hard for whatever it is you want in life," he said. "I'm staying true to my process."

 The 6-foot-2, 210-pound Doubs has been on the field for 65% of the offensive snaps, with only Hollins getting more playing time among receivers (72.5%). The Patriots have had to adjust after losing Brown, their No. 1 receiver, to a right high ankle sprain early in the third quarter of the Sept. 9 opener.

 Hollins, whose outgoing personality is the yin to Doubs' low-key yang, has enjoyed working with him.

 "Obviously, the physical ability speaks for itself; he's big, fast and strong," he said. "Just a guy in the room who is passionate about the game. His want for knowledge and to learn everything going on; he sees the bigger picture and boils it down to the smaller picture. That comes from years of work. It has stacked up, and it shows."

 Yet, the connection with Maye remains a work in progress. The quarterback lamented his third-down throw to Doubs early in the third quarter of last Sunday's blowout loss to the Jaguars, as Maye was trying to capitalize on one-on-one coverage along the sideline and left the ball inside.

 "I missed him, but love what he's been doing. He's just been putting his head down and working ever since the first game, and I'm gaining more and more trust in Romeo," Maye said.

 "He's doing some great things, blocking in the run game and joining in on the efforts of becoming what we like to do on offense for this football team with Coach [Mike] Vrabel, and that's effort, blocking downfield and doing the little things right. I'm really proud of how he has handled things and am looking forward to seeing him keep doing his thing."

 

 McDaniels said coaches can sometimes try to do too much with new players, and noted that there has been a process of identifying what Doubs does well and focusing on that first, with a goal to add more in time. He lauded Doubs' attitude in saying, "I think he has a really bright future here for us."

 Though Doubs has opted not to detail the differences for receivers in the Packers' and Patriots' offenses, he acknowledged the learning curve in New England.

 "It's a grind. It's not something I expected to happen quickly," he said. "Being in a new offense, it's a process. I'm staying true to it, and I look forward to my day-to-day work."

 2. WRs open: Patriots wide receivers and tight ends rank fifth in ESPN Analytics' open score metric through three games, and it reflects, in part, that getting open isn't among the most pressing issues for the NFL's lowest-scoring offense. For every route run, open score assesses the likelihood a receiver would complete a catch if he were targeted.

 3. Maye's decisions:  Maye, who has a league-high six interceptions, continues to stress that improving his decision-making is the first thing that can help revive the offense, as that's what "makes or breaks" quarterbacks.

 "I don't feel like we're going out there, getting outmatched and not moving the football. There are plays out there to be made," he said. "It starts with me making them go and making good decisions."

 4. Stat check:  Here's a deeper dive into stats that give context into Maye's struggles, per ESPN Research:

 
 His average time before pass this season is 3.04 seconds, up from 2.97 seconds last season. 
 He has faced pressure on 41.4% of dropbacks thus far, up from 33.9% in 2025. That is despite being blitzed at similar rates (30.0% in 2025; 29.3% in 2026). 
 Maye operated out of play-action on 24.8% of his dropbacks in 2025, a figure that has dropped to 19.2% this season. Maye led the NFL in QBR when using play-action last season, throwing 10 touchdowns and no interceptions on those plays. 
 After facing zone on 51% of his dropbacks last season, that has jumped to 65% this season. He's seeing a lot more Cover 2, up from 19% of his dropbacks last season to 32% this year. 
 
 5. New RG: In 2025, the Patriots had the sixth-most continuity in terms of starting offensive lines. This year, they'll already be breaking in their third different starting configuration in Week 4, with Ben Brown anticipated to start at right guard in place of the injured Mike Onwenu (ankle) and Greg Van Roten (thigh), according to Vrabel.

 Brown, whose most natural position is center, has never started an NFL game at the position but noted that he played there in last season's second game against the Jets. "I feel comfortable there," he said.

 

 6. Gilliam's return: Fullback Reggie Gilliam  spent the first six years of his career with the Bills before joining the Patriots this year. Here's what he said before the game:

 
 Returning to play in Orchard Park, New York: "Excited. To play in the new stadium and see my old teammates and old friends and everybody over there, it's a great opportunity and great experience, all around." 
 Greatest memories with the Bills: "Oh man, there's so many. AFC championships, making the playoffs every year I was there, just hanging out with the guys after practice, after games. I was there for six years; that's a big part of my life. So excited to see those guys, but at the end of the day, they're still the opponent, and we have to go out there and do what we do." 
 Thinking of this day when joining the Patriots: "I was excited to sign, of course, but it hurt leaving what I had known for so long -- my friends, my house, all the relationships I made out there. At the end of the day, it's a business and hardly anyone stays on the same team their whole career. I knew it was bound to happen at some point." 
 What he has learned about New England: "I've come to learn it's similar. It's a big family experience here. We're all close. We're all brothers. It's just one of those things that I think is pretty general across NFL locker rooms. You spend so much time with these guys, and I'm looking forward to continuing to grow those relationships." 
 
 7. Eyes on KR: Could Kyle Williams ' regrettable decision to field a kickoff at the 9-yard line and step out of bounds last week lead the coaching staff to consider a change?

 It didn't sound like special teams coordinator Jeremy Springer was thinking along those lines. He complimented Williams' overall body of work last week, but Efton Chism III is among the options if they make a change. Chism highlighted his kickoff mentality, saying, "Try to make an explosive play ... hit it and run through the smoke as hard…

title: Jameis Winston has time to prove he's the New York Giants' starter
summary: The Giants might have more patience with Winston than expected as the locker room believes in him implicitly.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- J.J. McCarthy 's first week with the New York Giants is being spent as the third-string quarterback. He arrived after being traded from the Minnesota Vikings for a fifth-round pick and begins behind veteran Jameis Winston and Jake Haener .

 Being the third-stringer seems like a temporary thing given his pedigree and the situation. The likelihood is that McCarthy will climb the depth chart once he learns the new offense and gets acclimated to his surroundings. He will either be the backup to Winston or eventually become the team's starter.

 It's all dependent on how Winston plays at home on Sunday against the Arizona Cardinals  ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ) and likely next week on the road against the Washington Commanders . He'll have to play better than he did against the Los Angeles Rams or Tennessee Titans . It could be considered a two-week tryout.

 Coach John Harbaugh says he is worried about this week and this week only. He even wore a black shirt with big white letters at Wednesday's practice that read "1-0" to accentuate that point.

 

 Winston, a 12-year veteran, knows how this all works. 

 "I have to play well regardless. That's it," he said emphatically on Wednesday. "It doesn't matter who's in the building. When you're the quarterback for the New York Football Giants, you have to give your team a chance to win. That's just the business that we're in."

 The Giants (2-1) are in a position at the moment where they can be patient. Harbaugh didn't feel the need to talk with Winston this week about trading for McCarthy and the status of his starting job.

 Harbaugh did say early in the week that it was going to be "a challenge" for McCarthy to learn the playbook. They'll see how he does and then determine whether he'll jump Haener on the depth chart against Arizona.

 But while McCarthy is talented and was selected in the top 10 of the 2024 NFL draft, there is no guarantee he will pick up the offense quickly. And even if he does, who says that McCarthy can play at a level higher than Winston and deserve to be the starter? There are still questions about what he truly is as a quarterback at the NFL level.

 One thing is certain: Winston will have to play better than he has in his first two games this season. He has a 22.9 QBR, dead last by a wide margin among the 30 qualifying quarterbacks. Only the Chargers' Justin Herbert (27.4) is below 35.0.

 Winston also has a 29.2% off-target percentage on his 49 pass attempts. That is also the worst among all quarterbacks.

 The 32-year-old is convinced there is plenty left in his arm.

 

 "Yeah, I know what I'm capable of, but also I know what's required of me," Winston said. "I can make all the throws. I can do anything I put my mind to. I'm blessed to that point. But at the same time, my job is to give the team the best chance to win."

 Winston led the Giants to a win on Sunday against the Titans. He pointed out it's hypocritical to criticize him for losing and throwing interceptions while racking up big yardage totals but not give him credit for doing what is necessary to win. Harbaugh also noted he won't be playing in a nor'easter every week, as was the case against the Titans. 

 Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy attributes this past week's misses to user error and the weather.

 "There's a little bit of the sinker ball that with a couple of the low throws that he had over the middle of the field. Jameis will tell you that. ... And it wasn't easy. It was misting and raining a little bit," Nagy said. "But I think Jameis will also be the first to tell you that's not an excuse. So mechanically, Jameis knows to keep that wide base to be able to throw through the throw and be able to make a friendlier catch for some of these passes."

 The Giants might have more patience with Winston than most seem to expect. The locker room believes in him implicitly. They saw last season during his two-start stint that he can play at a fairly high level. His performance on the road against the Detroit Lions (18-of-36 for 366 yards with two TDs passing and one receiving) was evidence.

 New York also thought several weeks ago he was among the league's best backup quarterbacks when it signed him to a two-year extension . It guaranteed Winston more than $6 million next season. That's not the type of commitment to make in a quarterback you don't believe can play.

 McCarthy already looked like a quarterback this week who was willing to learn from Winston. He was doing static stretching and bear crawls with Winston on the field long after his first practice as a Giant ended.

 But McCarthy comes to New York with more than just questions about his maturity. He was third among all qualifying quarterbacks last season with a 19.3% off-target rate. His QBR of 36.1 was only above Geno Smith 's 34.5 for the Las Vegas Raiders .

 Many of the concerns that led to the Giants passing on McCarthy in the draft were noticeable in his on-field performance for Minnesota. But as Harbaugh noted, McCarthy was a "top-10 pick for a reason." He has talent. The Giants are going to see if they can work with that.

 It will be as a contingency for Winston, for now.

 "It's an opportunity for us to improve our team, one little way maybe," Harbaugh said. "And who knows where it goes or where it doesn't go. ... I mean, he had a really good practice. Seems like he picked things up we asked him to pick up really well. Was in here late, early, studying, learning. [He] has a really good football foundation, all that kind of stuff. And that's exciting. It's another good football player at an important position."

title: Jets rookie Kenyon Sadiq has been a necessity instead of a 'luxury' draft pick
summary: New York used its second (No. 16) of three first-round picks on the tight end out of Oregon.
full_text:
CHICAGO -- A look at what's happening around the New York Jets :

 1.Breakout star: When they drafted tight end  Kenyon Sadiq with the 16th overall choice one year after taking a tight end in the second round, the Jets were criticized for making a "luxury" pick.

 It took only three games for Sadiq to go from luxury to necessity, especially with mounting injuries on offense.

 "He's uncoverable," wide receiver Garrett Wilson said of the rookie, whose size (6-foot-3, 241 pounds) and speed (sub 4.4 seconds in the 40-yard dash) make him a tough cover.

 

 Opponents are trying to figure him out. They've used linebackers on him (28 pass routes), along with safeties (19 routes) and cornerbacks (17 routes), per Next Gen Stats, citing closest-defender metrics.

 Offensive coordinator Frank Reich has moved Sadiq around the formation, making it harder for defenses to get a bead on him. On his 24-yard touchdown catch last week, the former Oregon star was covered by Detroit Lions cornerback Roger McCreary out of the slot.

 Told that it's unusual for a tight end to beat a corner that far downfield, Sadiq replied, "I feel that's kind of expected. I wouldn't say expected, but that's something I feel like I should be able to do, just with my skill set."

 Reich didn't expect Sadiq to make an impact this quickly, not after missing training camp with a hernia injury, but "he's a football player." That's coachspeak for, "He's tough, smart and he gets it."

 "I think I'm more excited about that," Reich said, "than the big numbers."

 The numbers were big last Sunday -- seven receptions for 105 yards and his first NFL touchdown catch. (He had a rushing TD in Week 1.) With running back Breece Hall , wide receiver Adonai Mitchell and tight end Mason Taylor out Sunday against the Chicago Bears , the Jets may need another prolific day from Sadiq, whose energy fuels the offense.

 "It's fun to watch him out there," Wilson said. "He's trying to jump over dudes and then, 'Oh, s---, didn't work. Guess I'll just keep running.' S--- like that gets me hyped, bro, I'm not going to lie. I'll be on the field just laughing like, 'Hell, yeah, bro!'"

 

 2. On the edge: Will McDonald IV 's name is sure to make its way into the rumor mill as the Nov. 10 trade deadline approaches.

 The 2023 first-round pick drew interest last year, when he had a full-time role on defense. Now he's a rotational player whose playing time could be shrinking.

 Joseph Ossai 's return last week created a five-man rotation at edge rusher, with rookie David Bailey , Kingsley Enagbare and Braiden McGregor manning the other spots. All but McGregor participated in more defensive snaps than McDonald, whose pass-rushing production has cratered after a promising Week 1 (no QB hits in the last two games).

 McDonald played 61% of the defensive snaps last season; he's down to 41%. It's a new scheme and a new position, which could explain his slow start.

 Edge rushers always have value, and perhaps there's a contending team that believes he still can be the player that made 10.5 sacks in 2024. Coach Aaron Glenn said McDonald is "a huge part of what we're doing," but that can always change.

 The Jets' willingness to trade him, or any player for that matter, could hinge on their place in the standings at the deadline. McDonald's fifth-year option was exercised, so he's signed through 2027 ($13.8 million guaranteed). An extension seems unlikely, so it might behoove them to get what they can before he walks in 2028.

 3. Rare lineup change: The offensive line will have a different look Sunday. For the first time in 21 games, the Jets won't have their five regular starters. They were the only team last season to start the same five in every game.

 Now left guard Dylan Parham (knee) is sidelined , disrupting the remarkable run of good fortune. Former Las Vegas Raiders starter Jordan Meredith , who missed the blitz pick-up last week that resulted in Geno Smith 's sack-fumble, is expected to replace Parham.

 4. Bailey in coverage: Many fans probably are aghast whenever Bailey drops into pass coverage. The most accomplished pass rusher in the 2026 draft already has logged 15 coverage snaps, including eight last week. Yes, eight!

 Defensive coordinator Brian Duker defended the idea of dropping edge defenders, saying it adds "flexibility and creativity" to the scheme. He noted that Bailey was in coverage on Andre Cisco 's sack on a safety blitz, claiming the wrinkle allowed them to overload one side of the Lions' protection.

 

 5. At the Mendoza line: Glenn reached the 20-game mark with only four wins. He's one of only nine coaches since 2000 to have a .200 winning percentage or worse in his first 20 games with the same team, according to ESPN Research.

 Statistically, the chances of a turnaround are remote. Of the previous eight, only one -- the Cincinnati Bengals ' Zac Taylor -- achieved sustained success after his dreadful start. Jim Schwartz did get the Lions to the playoffs in his third year, but he followed that with two losing seasons and was a goner.

 It's worth noting that the Lions' Dan Campbell (.225) narrowly missed the list and has proved that a major reversal is possible. Glenn, who rode shotgun with Campbell as his defensive coordinator, has compared the current Jets to those Lions, even saying after last week's game that he's experiencing "déjà vu."

 The Lions finished 9-8 in Campbell's second year, so Glenn's turnaround needs to start soon.

 6. Where's Wright? Nahshon Wright returns to Chicago, where he recorded five interceptions last season -- tied for most in the league by a cornerback. He has no big plays yet in New York; it's hard to make plays when you're not on the field.

 A healthy scratch last week, Wright has logged 18 snaps -- all on special teams, none on defense. It seems odd that the team with the longest interception drought (20 games) in NFL history can't find a spot for a ball hawk, but such is life in the Jets' secondary.

 "You have to be a pro," Wright said. "It's not my first rodeo. It's not my first time being inactive."

 Wright is on a one-year, $3.5 million contract, fully guaranteed.

 7. Did you know? The Jets have one or fewer wins entering October for the ninth time in last 11 seasons, two more times than any other team since 2016.

 

 8. Not their kind of town: The Jets haven't won in Chicago since 1997, Bill Parcells' first year as coach. Since then, they are 0-3 at Soldier Field.

 9. Early return: Three games isn't enough time to draw a conclusion on a trade, but let's peek at the T'Vondre Sweat - Jermaine Johnson II  swap anyway -- a rare player-for-player trade. Johnson is off to a poor start with the Tennessee Titans -- zero sacks, zero quarterback hits and a 0.0% pass rush win rate, per ESPN Analytics.

 Johnson, who likes to call himself an apex predator, has been anything but. Sweat's job is to stuff the run the run. He hasn't made any eye-popping plays, but he has seven run tackles in 38 runs snaps, per Next Gen Stats -- not a bad ratio for a nose tackle. Perhaps more telling: The Jets allow 3.7 yards per rush when he's on the field and 5.1 when he's not.

 Early trade analysis? Slight advantage, Jets. 

 10. The Last Word: "I think you guys have seen 'Hard Knocks,' so just go back and watch that." -- Glenn on his relationship with Bears coach Ben Johnson, who served with Glenn on Campbell's Detroit staff. In 2022, the Lions were featured on HBO's "Hard Knocks," which showed highly competitive practices (with lots of trash-talking) between Glenn's defense and Johnson's offense.

title: Philadelphia Eagles' defense at an inflection point
summary: With the next four games against formidable offenses, this stretch will help define whether Philly's defense is for real -- or just real good on paper.
full_text:
The Eagles' offense was expected to be a work in progress under first-year offensive coordinator Sean Mannion . The thinking went that the defense could serve as the team's bedrock while the other side of the ball found its way.

 With the star-studded cast entering Year 3 under one of the greats in defensive coordinator Vic Fangio, this group seemed to have top-five defense written all over it.

 It was jarring to watch a projected juggernaut get shredded in real time Monday night, as 38-year-old third-string quarterback Case Keenum  completed 71 percent of his passes, threw two touchdowns and ran for another in his first start in 1,009 days, leading the Bears to a 27-7 rout over Philadelphia.

 "It just can't happen," Eagles edge Jonathan Greenard  said. "We know what the standard is, we know we've got to be better, and we will be better, so I'm not worried."

 There is plenty of season left to turn the tide, but with a string of offensive powers coming up, starting with the Los Angeles Rams Sunday (1 pm ET, Fox), this defense finds itself at an early inflection point.

 Every unit has a bad day at the office, and Bears coach Ben Johnson has left many a defense soul-searching after an encounter. But the overall numbers through three weeks are less than encouraging.

 

 To start, the Eagles have zero takeaways. It's the first time in franchise history they've been blanked over the first three weeks of the season. They are the only team in the NFL that hasn't generated a turnover.

 The Eagles have managed just three sacks, tied for the fourth-lowest output in the league. They are 23 rd in defensive efficiency (42.16) and opposing quarterback rating (64.1), 22 nd in defensive EPA (-10.30) and 25 th in opponent rushing yards per game (127.3).

 There are a multitude of reasons for the slow start. At the top of the list is that some of the stars are not playing like stars. Defensive tackle Jalen Carter , fresh off a four-year, $152 million extension, has been wearing a cast on his hand for the last two weeks as he reportedly deals with a hairline fracture in his wrist . Defensive back Cooper DeJean got off to a slow start as he dealt with calf and abdomen injuries. Linebacker Zack Baun , in contrast, started off strong but had a down night against Chicago. He has been sidelined at practice this week with a concussion.

 Their big offseason acquisition, Greenard, was on a pitch count in his debut against the Bears after missing extended time with a pec injury.

 There has been some turnover at key starting spots, and that has come with an acclimation period. The early returns have been generally positive on corner Riq Woolen , but a breakdown between him and DeJean led to Kalif Raymond being left wide open for a 41-yard touchdown in the second half Monday night.

 "We've got to communicate better, make sure everybody gets the call, get everyone on the same page so we don't leave guys running free," DeJean said.

 Two of the defense's top communicators in linebacker Nakobe Dean and safety Reed Blankenship are now in Las Vegas and Houston, respectively. Former first-round pick Jihaad Campbell is still settling in at the starting linebacker spot opposite Baun, and there's been a rotating cast at safety, with Marcus Epps and Michael Carter II now splitting reps opposite Andrew Mukuba , who has been dealing with a knee injury.

 The safety spot in particular has become problematic. Interestingly, the Eagles signed former Pro Bowl defensive back Kenny Moore II to the practice squad last week and have since elevated him to the active roster. He primarily played in the slot during his nine years with the Indianapolis Colts but has been working at safety since coming to Philly.

 While Moore is motivated to make his mark in a new city as he did in Indianapolis, Fangio said "he's a down the line possibility, maybe" as he gets used to a new position.

 It's not all doom and gloom on the defensive side of the ball. The Eagles might only have three sacks but are tied for 10 th in pressures (40) and now have Greenard back, offering hope that they can turn the corner there. Mukuba and DeJean are both off the injury report, which can only help a passing defense that ranks ninth in yards per game (193).

 And with a little work, perhaps the back seven can turn pass breakups into interceptions before long.

 "We've just got to keep giving them multiple ball drills. Coaches throwing ball drills is almost a waste because they're lollipops," Fangio said. "We've got to get them on the jugs or get a real quarterback throwing them some balls that have some RPMs, maybe like a [Phillies closer Jhoan] Duran fastball rather than a Jamie Moyer."

 But the turnaround has to start now. With the next four games against formidable offenses in the Rams, Jacksonville Jaguars , Carolina Panthers and Dallas Cowboys , this stretch will help define whether this defense is for real, or just real good on paper.
